entries.title: Amy Sherald Would Rather Walk Away Than Water Down Her Art
entries.author: Belinda Luscombe
paragraphs: Nobody knows in advance the moment that will change everything, but some of Amy Sherald’s friends sensed something was up. The artist had been called to meet Barack and Michelle Obama as they decided who would paint their official portraits. Her best friend’s mother insisted on taking her to MaxMara and buying her a taupe sheath and kitten heels. When she walked into the Oval Office, both the President and the First Lady were wearing the same color. The President quipped that she must have gotten the memo. Sherald did not get the joke. But she did get the job that changed her life: the portrait of Michelle Obama that is the highlight of “American Sublime,” the blockbuster show of Sherald’s work that is just finishing an almost two-year, four-museum national tour.

Color has always been important to Sherald, as anyone with even a brief acquaintance with her paintings can tell. She paints all her canvases red before she paints them gray. “I think color lives whether you can see it or not,” she says in her Jersey City, N.J., studio, a few feet from a giant pegboard filled with hundreds of paint tubes held up by bulldog clips. “So I consider the red kind of like the blood behind the figures there.” Maybe that’s why, even though she paints everyone in gray tones, Sherald’s people pulse with life. Sometimes they float off dirt bikes, or balance on tractors, or hold a doll or a baby or an outsize teacup, but mostly they command attention, looking evenly at the viewer, wearing bright clothes in front of a vivid background. “Color is my natural language,” says Sherald, 53. “Using my voice is only the third best way that I communicate.”

Her inspirations for the color and the composition of her work come from paintings, she says. But the subject matter is mostly inspired by photography, because that is what she grew up seeing, in family portraits and encyclopedias. Once she finds a subject, she photographs them in an outfit she has preselected. Often the clothing is the starting point. (She’s in the early stages of a work inspired by a vintage Girl Scouts uniform.) Despite her most famous painting, she doesn’t call herself a portraitist. “Once I take the photograph, the model just becomes a character in the world that I'm trying to create,” she says. “This is now a part of this greater picture and this greater story.”

Successful artists are the product of their gifts, but as Sherald proves, they are also products of what they lacked. Sherald grew up in a home that followed the teachings of the Worldwide Church of God, which did not celebrate, among other things, birthdays, Halloween, movies, most dancing, and TV. Her home kept a Sabbath on Saturdays. Not that Sherald minded. “For me as a child who was self-conscious and introverted, I would choose to stay in and draw rather than go outside,” she says. “It was like a safe way to play that was not with other people.” Her father, a dentist, was diagnosed with Parkinson's when she was 7. She would often just sit with him. “When you have a parent that doesn't communicate well and they're also going through something they want to hide from you, it kind of opens up another way of learning about emotion and communication.”

Famously, it was on a school trip that Sherald saw Bo Bartlett’s painting Object Permanence, centered on a Black man in a tool belt, which inspired her to depict Black people as she saw them. “It was just about looking. Looking back at our history and painting the things that I didn't see,” she says. “Art history tells me that I'm elevating my people, but I'm not. That's just the story that's projected onto my storytelling. They're already there.” She and Bartlett are now friends.

Recognition for Sherald’s work came slowly, then all at once. Just before she had her heart transplant, at 39, after she stopped waitressing to look after her brother, she sold a painting for $3,000. Her friends set up a GoFundMe page for her medical costs. “I'm sure some people were like, ‘Poor Amy, she wants to be an artist,’” she says. “‘She's still working at this restaurant, like it's obvious it's not gonna happen.’” In 2019, a year after the Obama portrait was unveiled, her work Innocent You, Innocent Me sold for $350,000 at Christie’s. A mere 18 months later, The Bathers netted $4.26 million at auction. She found the sudden uptick in wealth and fame difficult. “People don't think you've earned it,” she says. “And there's pressure to do more because you have this success.”

The heart transplant has made Sherald, who has books about overcoming anxiety in her office, even more cautious. She wanted to take up cycling but realized a fall could hurt her hand. She no longer rides roller coasters. She lost her father when she was 27 and brother to lung cancer when he was 38. Her sister also recently had a heart transplant. But if those health crises have made her wary, they did not make her scared. In 2025, after officials at the Smithsonian's National Portrait Gallery, the same institution that commissioned the Obama portrait, got skittish about exhibiting her painting Trans Forming Liberty, which features a trans woman, she pulled the show. “‘American Sublime’ has its own narrative,” she says. “Deviating from that narrative would be deviating from the core person of who I am and why the work exists in the world, and I just wasn't willing to do that.” The exhibition was snapped up by the Baltimore Museum of Art, where it broke attendance records.

Sherald, to quote the old gospel song, wouldn’t take nothing for her journey now. “There's only one person I've ever been envious of in my life, and that was Oprah Winfrey when she was giving away cars to people,” she says. “I want to be able to do that. I want someone to give me enough money that I can set up a big foundation where there's rolling grants for artists for medical care, for housing, for studios. Because that's all we need to become who we want to be: time and money.” In the meantime, she’s delighted by the life she has been given. “I think,” she says, “art definitely chose me.”

entries.title: JR
entries.author: Isa Farfan
paragraphs: French street artist JR is guided by one question: Can art change the world? The inquiry doubles as the name of his foundation, which supports community art programs. This summer, JR (a moniker of his given name, Jean-René) wrapped Paris’s oldest bridge in fabric, for the monumental public installation La Caverne Du Pont Neuf. The 13-day project made the bridge look like a craggy mountainscape and created a cave-like atmosphere inside. It was designed, he says, to invite the city to slow down and resist “overconnected” modern life. Other works by the artist have taken a more overt political tone. His 2017 mural Kikito featured a giant portrait of a real-life toddler peering over the border fence between California and Tecate, Mexico. In 2019, he worked with incarcerated people to create a mural in the yard of a California prison; seven years later, JR’s nonprofit has brought similar arts instruction to about 4,000 prisons worldwide. On Sept. 14, Pope Leo XIV inaugurated JR’s installation of a colossal wave inside the Vatican’s Apostolic Library, a commentary on the threats of war and climate change to knowledge. “All my work, even in the most violent zones … has always been about light, about people, about hope,” JR says. “It's in times like now, even more, we need artists to remind us of our humanity.”

entries.title: Bonnie Brennan
entries.author: Belinda Luscombe
paragraphs: A longtime auction executive who was promoted to CEO of Christie’s in 2025, Bonnie Brennan has been given the unglamorous task of guiding the 260-year-old house through a protracted art-market slump. Under her watch, Christie’s saw sales rise 71% over the prior year in the first half of 2026, following three years of uneven returns. In May, Christie’s New York sold a record $1.45 billion worth of art from the estates of prominent collectors including media mogul S.I. Newhouse, and philanthropist Agnes Gund. Brennan, 53, has taken a particular interest in supporting the market for works by women, giving pride of place to examples by Joan Mitchell and Alice Neel. She’s also bullish on the future of the auction business. “For the younger generation, because of their focus on sustainability and shopping with values and ethics, there’s a real opportunity for the secondhand market,” she said in December, noting that the median value of a Christie’s lot is just $8,000.

entries.title: Taryn Simon
entries.author: Taylor Dafoe
paragraphs: Taryn Simon made her name by turning her eye to what goes unseen all around us, whether she’s photographing goods seized as contraband at JFK airport or creating portraits of people who were wrongfully convicted. In recent years, she’s expanded her toolkit to include video, text, and sculpture, as she dives deeper into the invisible structures of power that shape our lives and reverberate through different cultures. “To get to the finish line takes every ounce of me,” she says of her exhaustive projects. In September, at the Guggenheim in New York City, she will present her largest show to date, featuring artworks that follow the life of an unidentified federal agent. The building’s iconic spiral offers a ready metaphor for Simon’s career. After years spent following her digressive interests into government buildings, nuclear waste facilities, wildlife rescues, and other odd corners of the world, Simon, 51, has finally reached the top. But there is further still to go: she will also unveil a large-scale public project in Times Square next spring.

entries.title: Kerry James Marshall
entries.author: Katie White
paragraphs: If old-fashioned-seeming genres like history painting and portraiture have begun to feel fresh again, you can thank Kerry James Marshall. Growing up, Marshall was acutely aware of the absence of Black artists and subjects in visual culture ranging from comic books to art museums. His paintings, which riff on masterpieces that depicted daily life from Velázquez to Manet, offer a correction to such erasures. Set in barbershops, parks, and amusement parks, and populated by figures with deep Black skin, his images illustrate how artists can adapt the tools and concepts of art history to offer fresh insight into contemporary life. “You have to demonstrate that black is richer than it appears to be, that it is not just darkness but a color,” Marshall has said. In 2018, his painting Past Times (1997) sold at auction for a record-breaking $21.1 million. That painting recently appeared in the largest presentation of Marshall’s work outside of the U.S., a major survey that traveled from the Royal Academy of Arts in London to Kunsthaus Zürich, and this fall heads to the Musée d'Art Moderne de Paris. More is on the horizon: in 2027, the Print Center New York will open the first comprehensive exhibition of his lesser-known print practice.

entries.title: Wolfgang Tillmans
entries.author: Naomi Rea
paragraphs: Wolfgang Tillmans has relentlessly pushed the boundaries of photography. A decade before camera phones, he recognized the power of capturing unguarded portraits of LGTBQIA+ people and their communities, helping to destigmatize queer life during the AIDS crisis. The German artist also pioneered a style of colorful abstract chemical prints that have become among the most sought-after contemporary photographs, with auction prices surpassing $750,000.

Since he became the first photographer (and first non-British artist) to win the Turner Prize in 2000, Tillmans’ images have infiltrated pop culture, gracing more than 50 book and album covers, including Frank Ocean’s Blonde. His Between Bridges foundation, started in 2017, supports LGBTQIA+ rights and anti-racist activism.

Following a critically lauded 2025 survey at the Pompidou in Paris, “Nothing Could Have Prepared Us—Everything Could Have Prepared Us,” Tillmans opened a solo show at the city’s Galerie Chantal Crousel in September, and is included in two major international biennials. In May, he won the $185,000 Roswitha Haftmann Prize, Europe’s largest monetary art award, affirming his status as one of today’s most potent photographers.

entries.title: Jennifer Rubio
entries.author: Belinda Luscombe
paragraphs: Although she’s been seriously collecting art for less than a decade, Jen Rubio has made an impression on the fine art world similar to the one she made on luggage when she co-founded the Away suitcase brand in 2015. She acknowledges the impact of her collection, which is more than half by female artists and has helped elevate historically undervalued figures, but says her choices were primarily from the heart. “I didn't set out to collect women Surrealists because I felt I needed to support the estates of these women who were not getting their due,” she says. “The art is just so good.” In April, she and her soon-to-be-ex-husband, the tech billionaire Stewart Butterfield, also pledged more than $23 million to the Metropolitan Museum of Art, where she sits on the board, to ensure that the august institution can always pay its interns. “I've always been really fascinated by interventions that happen early enough to be able to to change the trajectory of someone's life,” she says. The couple also helped several museums buy works that they loved but would not otherwise have been able to afford. “Collecting has really just been about what I want to live with,” she says. “Philanthropy is about what I want to outlive me.”

entries.title: Cao Fei
entries.author: Naomi Rea
paragraphs: If artists help us see the future, few have had a better track record than Cao Fei. One of China’s best-known artists and a new-media pioneer, her work has predicted the latest iterations of the kind of paradoxes that have accompanied technological progress from the industrial revolution to the AI era. In 2018, she filmed a video inside a Chinese logistics center that prefigured the Amazon warehouses that now dot the globe; one character in this fictional near-future has a barcode on her wrist, a nod to the careful surveillance of worker productivity. Her nearly 30-year catalog of films, virtual reality experiences, and installations examining everything from factory life to the metaverse fuels a survey exhibition, “Testimonies to the Near Future,” on view through October at the Kunstmuseum Basel in Switzerland.

Her latest body of work, showing at Milan’s Fondazione Prada through September, probes how deployment of smart technology at farms across China and Southeast Asia is both enhancing efficiency and displacing traditional knowledge. Drawing on three years of fieldwork and research, “Dash” invites viewers to step into a surreal environment that visualizes the way algorithms are changing humanity’s relationship to the land.

entries.title: David Zwirner
entries.author: Tim Schneider
paragraphs: The German second-generation dealer David Zwirner has built an empire by blending old-school refinement and calculated risk-taking. Known for championing a museum-approved cross-section of postwar and contemporary artists, his gallery has recently shaken up its image by signing ascendant millennial and Gen Z talent including Yu Nishimura, Sasha Gordon, and Louis Fratino. Since 2022, his gallery has also lured away from rivals multiple blue-chip names, like German painter Gerhard Richter, the estate of American sculptor Robert Therrien, and Japanese artist Yoshitomo Nara, whose first show with Zwirner will open in New York this fall.

Yet what separates Zwirner, whose business now spans 10 locations in four countries, from his mega-gallerist peers is his focus on efficiency and brand-building. Two stints working with McKinsey and Goldman Sachs veteran Suki Larson over the past 20 years helped shape his business strategy. He has also invested in unconventional tools (at least among art dealers) to reach new audiences, including a podcast, ongoing since 2018, and digital sales infrastructure. Staying on top, Zwirner recognizes, requires more than taste and hustle.

entries.title: Charles Stewart
entries.author: Tim Schneider
paragraphs: When telecom tycoon Patrick Drahi acquired Sotheby’s in 2019, he raised eyebrows by naming Charles Stewart the now 282-year-old auction house’s chief executive. Stewart, 56, had a long career in banking and corporate leadership but had never worked in the art world. Fast forward to 2026, and he is the longest-tenured current head of a major auction house. He’s also managed some growth within a challenging market.

Under Stewart, Sotheby’s has opened a new Hong Kong flagship featuring a retail boutique and, in November, relocated its New York headquarters to a landmarked Madison Avenue building whose past tenants include the Whitney, the Met, and the Frick Collection. He has expanded Sotheby’s ties to the Gulf, securing around $1 billion of investment from Abu Dhabi’s sovereign wealth fund in late 2024 and launching live sales in Saudi Arabia in 2025—a first for a Western auction house. The firm’s offerings have diversified, too, expanding further into collectibles and even taking a controlling stake in collectible cars specialist RM Auctions. It seems the CEO’s outsider thinking has paid off: altogether, Sotheby’s sold nearly $50 billion of art and luxury collectibles in Stewart’s first seven years.

entries.title: Anne Imhof
entries.author: Naomi Rea
paragraphs: Anne Imhof has introduced a new era of performance art with slow-moving, bass-pounding tableaux that captivate even today’s media-addled attention spans. The German artist had one of the most talked-about artistic projects of 2025 with Doom: House of Hope, her three-hour epic performance loosely based on Romeo and Juliet. The event, which cast Balenciaga models alongside professional ballet dancers, drew 9,000 visitors across its 10 dates at the Park Avenue Armory in New York City. Imhof’s angsty-cool aesthetic has made her a darling of fashion brands and European museum curators alike. In the past year, she also co-starred in Valentino’s Cruise 2026 fashion campaign and unveiled a monumental permanent public sculpture of a swimming pool outside the Serralves Museum of Contemporary Art in Porto, Portugal. In September, she will open her first solo show in Asia: a survey exhibition at Hong Kong’s Tai Kwun center, where signature works will be shown alongside a new performance in collaboration with the Hong Kong Ballet.

entries.title: Hank Willis Thomas
entries.author: Caroline Goldstein
paragraphs: In Philadelphia, a massive Afro pick with a handle in the shape of a clenched fist stands as a monument to Black resilience. The sculpture, titled All Power to All People, is emblematic of the work of Hank Willis Thomas, a conceptual artist whose practice often subverts the iconography of pop culture and mass media to, as he likes to say, “re-right” history. With art in prominent public spaces like the Boston Common and downtown Brooklyn, Thomas embodies what civic engagement can look like for an artist looking to express the complexity of American society. For Freedoms, a collective he co-founded in 2016, has installed more than 500 artist-designed billboards around the country, which encourage people to vote and get involved in their communities. In October, Thomas unveiled a sculpture memorializing the enslaved people who built Davidson College in North Carolina. “The road to progress is always under construction.” Thomas told TIME in 2025. “We're trying to not go back.”

entries.title: Hoor Al Qasimi
entries.author: Naomi Rea
paragraphs: Hoor Al Qasimi is a connector. Since age 22, when she first organized the Sharjah Biennial in the UAE emirate where her father rules, the curator has helped turn the once modest local art show into a closely-watched global exhibition. Driven by a belief that “culture bridges gaps and brings people together,” Al Qasimi has promoted international contemporary art as president and director of Sharjah Art Foundation, one of her many institutional roles. Now 46, her willingness to platform diverse ideas has projected an intellectually progressive image for a principality that is often viewed as the most conservative of the region, earning her fans and detractors alike. A signature annual initiative, March Meeting, brings together artists, curators, and theorists for three days of spirited conversation and debate. As the artistic director of the Sydney Biennale this year, Al Qasimi spotlighted powerful work by Indigenous, Palestinian, and Iranian artists, which earned praise from critics for delving into work that’s often marginalized.

In recognition of her contributions to cross-cultural dialogue, in November she was entrusted with a diplomatic role as “ambassador extraordinary” by the Arab League Educational, Cultural and Scientific Organization. In an unstable region, “the more we can try to connect, the better,” she says. It’s a philosophy she channels into her expansive public work. In July, she became president of Sharjah Museums Authority, where she will work to develop a cohesive strategy for the emirate’s network of 16 museums and heritage houses. It brings her job count up to nine, including stewarding four cultural institutions and two universities.

entries.title: Christopher A. Marinello
entries.author: Naomi Rea
paragraphs: It's a bad day for art thieves when Christopher Marinello is on the case. After years of litigating stolen art cases for wealthy collectors in court, the lawyer saw an appetite for a solution that was faster, cheaper, and more discreet. In 2013 he founded specialist practice Art Recovery International to provide due diligence, dispute resolution, and art recovery services to private collectors, governments, and art businesses. He now works the seams between clients, private investigators, and underworld sources to track down stolen work by the likes of Warhol, Matisse, and Van Gogh. Over three decades, Marinello estimates he has recovered more than $500 million worth of cultural heritage, including identifying a Picasso aquatint stolen in 1990 from a Texas oil executive that was returned to an heir of the victim in March.

At a moment when thefts are getting more brazen, everyone from museum security to law enforcement is scrambling for answers. Even a fortress like the Louvre has proved vulnerable, as the October 2025 smash-and-grab heist of the French crown jewels made clear. When he’s not working for private clients, Marinello estimates about half of his time is spent doing pro bono work for museums, an area of his practice that has been growing.

entries.title: Suhanya Raffel
entries.author: Naomi Rea
paragraphs: The director of M+ in Hong Kong, Suhanya Raffel has navigated a whole career’s worth of challenges in just five years since it opened. The museum she leads focuses on visual and digital culture, with recent exhibitions considering the internet’s influence on video art and the relationship between Picasso and four generations of Asian and Asian diasporic artists. Raffel opened the transdisciplinary institution during the COVID pandemic, in 2021, only to face growing government censorship and a funding crisis. She has defended the need for artistic independence while operating under Hong Kong's national security law, which criminalizes anything deemed critical of China's government, including art. Raffel has made strides in increasing private fundraising (M+ raised HKD130,000,000, or $16.6 million, in 2025), an ever-more-valuable skill amid shrinking public funding and mounting scrutiny in Hong Kong.

At the same time, Raffel has managed to establish the museum’s global credibility, overseeing 15 major collaboration agreements to create ongoing exchanges of resources and research beyond one-off shows or loans, including recent deals with New York City’s Museum of Modern Art and Paris’s Centre Pompidou. Under the latter deal, the institutions will team up to commission new art and present a series of exhibitions in Hong Kong starting next year.

entries.title: Dayanita Singh
entries.author: Katie White
paragraphs: Dayanita Singh creates images that pulse with life. The Indian photographer is known for unfiltered shots of local shopkeepers, strangers, and friends and family. Her photographs offer a dynamic and evolving portrait of India over nearly 40 years through often unorthodox methods. In a 2022 interview, she likened her waist-level, medium-format Hasselblad camera to a “third breast,” noting her tendency to shoot from her core, “dancing around” her subjects, rather than standing still and looking down through the viewfinder. She’s been equally innovative in the presentation and distribution of her works, often displaying photographs in what she calls “mobile museums,” folding wooden structures that are portable, or on towers of cubes that can be continuously rearranged. Singh goes beyond traditional art-market approaches: in addition to selling limited-edition prints at high prices through a gallery, which is the typical approach for a fine-art photographer, she also creates more affordable photographic books and collections. Earlier this spring, Singh’s works were presented in a headline-making exhibition at the State Archives of Venice. This fall, she will open two more solo museum exhibitions in Rome and Turin.

entries.title: Ken Griffin
entries.author: Julia Halperin
paragraphs: “My first love in art was the proverbial one that got away,” says Ken Griffin, the CEO of the hedge fund Citadel. In 1999, he lost out on a sculpture of a dancer by the French Impressionist Edgar Degas. He has rarely let it happen again. Over the past two decades, Griffin has emerged as one of the world’s most dogged, deep-pocketed collectors. His treasures include Abstract Expressionist paintings worth nine figures, rare historical documents, and a Madonna and Child attributed to Leonardo da Vinci.

While Griffin previously lent many of his most valuable works to museums anonymously, he has expanded and become more public about his activities over the past year, a shift he says is designed to facilitate scholarship and education as well as satisfy public curiosity. He loaned the da Vinci to the Met this spring, doubling the number of paintings by the Renaissance master on view in the U.S.

The billionaire has also expanded his support of Florida museums since his much-publicized relocation to Miami from Chicago in 2022. Over the summer, an exhibition of 10 works by Jean-Michel Basquiat from his collection went on view at the Pérez Art Museum in Griffin’s new hometown. In 2027, he will place a Richard Serra sculpture he bought earlier this year on public display in a park next to the museum. “It’s monumental, it's thought-provoking, and, bluntly, it's just fun,” Griffin says of the work. “An institution has a different criteria to collect than I do as a private individual. I place a huge importance on the aesthetic appeal of a work. Does this work visually make me happy?”

entries.title: Noah Horowitz
entries.author: Tim Schneider
paragraphs: Without art fairs, today’s highly globalized and commercialized art world would not exist. While many galleries complain about the high cost and grueling travel required to participate in international trade shows, they also rely on them to expand their clientele and turn buying art into an event. As chief executive of Art Basel, the most famous brand in art fairs, Noah Horowitz understands this paradox well. Since he took on the role in 2022, he has doubled down on Art Basel’s core business, most visibly by allying with the Qatari royal family to launch the firm’s fifth annual fair in Doha this past February and shepherding its Paris show to the historic Grand Palais in 2024. But he has also expanded the brand’s reach in forward-looking ways, including by augmenting its fairs with the dedicated digital art section Zero 10 and a retail shop for branded and artist-created merchandise, as well as diversifying Art Basel’s partnerships lineup with big names like Miu Miu, Samsung, and Qatar Airways. “I felt there was more Art Basel could do proactively and creatively… to meet an evolving market where it was,” Horowitz says. Now, he and his team are “working double time” to get there.

entries.title: Stan Prokopenko
entries.author: Isa Farfan
paragraphs: Carrying the spirit of PBS art instructor Bob Ross into the digital age, 40-year-old Stan Prokopenko offers free sketching tutorials, anatomy lessons, and painting explainers on his YouTube channel, Proko. His following has grown exponentially since the start of the COVID pandemic, reaching nearly 4.4 million subscribers. While arts education budgets are squeezed across the U.S., Prokopenko, like his forefather Ross, warmly invites anyone—especially those with disabilities like arthritis—to learn to draw from the comfort of their homes. In addition to YouTube lessons, Prokopenko created his own profitable e-learning platform to host free and paid lessons (for up to about $200 each) taught by more than 160 arts educators. The Odessa, Ukraine-born artist brought in roughly $4 million in sales last year, including, the company reports, revenue from 80,000 paying Proko students. Whether he’s teaching gesture drawing or providing motivation, Prokopenko’s light-hearted YouTube videos attract vivid testimonials from users who say his content uplifted them, and even saved their lives.

entries.title: Myriam Ben Salah
entries.author: Sarah Cascone
paragraphs: If you want to find the next hot artist, you could do worse than scanning the list of upcoming exhibitions at the Renaissance Society, a small but widely influential art space at the University of Chicago. Since Myriam Ben Salah took over as director in 2020, the institution has staged shows by a litany of rising stars who went on to broader art-world acclaim, including Diane Severin Nguyen, Lydia Ourahmane, and Meriem Bennani. Ben Salah credits her sharp eye to her international and interdisciplinary background. Born in Algeria and raised in Tunisia, she speaks five languages and studied theater and philosophy in France before moving to the U.S. This year, she organized the French Pavilion at the Venice Biennale. “I'm very interested in the overlap between contemporary art and popular culture or between the avant-garde and the mainstream,” Ben Salah says. Upcoming exhibitions include a project with Spanish artist Antoni Miralda to be staged at a local restaurant, recreating the one he ran in New York in the 1980s.

entries.title: Olugbile Holloway
entries.author: Isa Farfan
paragraphs: In 1897, British troops sacked Benin City in modern-day Nigeria, and stole about 5,000 artifacts collectively known as the Benin Bronzes. Despite decades of calls for repatriation, many of these looted objects remained in museums in Europe and the U.S. until 2021, when some governments and institutions finally began to return them. Last June, Olugbile Holloway, the director-general of Nigeria’s National Commission for Museums and Monuments, facilitated one of the largest single repatriations of the looted Benin Bronzes to date: 119 objects from the Netherlands. In February, he oversaw the return of over 100 artifacts from the University of Cambridge to Nigeria.

According to Chika Okeke-Agulu, an expert in African diaspora art history, the historic agreement stems from Holloway’s ability to quell confusion both within Nigeria and abroad about the rightful owner of the bronzes. Holloway—whose background is in corporate advertising—says he and the Benin Oba, or monarch, adopted a 20-page agreement outlining shared commitments to the artifacts’ future. Because of that agreement, Holloway says, the Nigerian government presented a unified front in its request for the return of bronzes from the Netherlands. The director-general has now set his sights on negotiating the future of Nigerian antiquities at the British Museum, which is prohibited by law from deaccessioning its collection of bronzes.

entries.title: Dana Awartani
entries.author: Sarah Cascone
paragraphs: Can art offer a blueprint for healing? That’s the argument Dana Awartani, 39, makes in her work. The Saudi Arabian artist creates immersive installations of silk panels by ripping and “darning” (or repairing) the fabric. She also works with experts in ancient craft traditions to build installations that double as memorials to places destroyed by conflict. At this year’s Venice Biennale, she covered the floor of Saudi Arabia’s pavilion with 29,000 clay bricks, handmade by 32 master artisans, which referenced 23 damaged sites across the Levant. Entering the installation felt like being transported into an archaeological dig. Laid without binding agents, the floor was designed to crack over the course of the show’s run—an acknowledgement of the fragility of cultural heritage and the violence of erasure. Awartani, who trained in Islamic art traditions, will open solo shows at Lisson Gallery in London in November and Norway’s Stavanger Art Museum next year.

entries.title: Luke Nikas
entries.author: Julia Halperin
paragraphs: As the amount of money being spent by the art world has risen over the past 20 years, the number of lawsuits—over botched business deals, alleged fakes, and Nazi loot—has grown in tandem. Luke Nikas has emerged as the art world’s go-to lawyer for some of its most bitter disputes. In the past decade, the partner at the firm Quinn Emanuel Urquhart & Sullivan has played key roles in a scandal over approximately $70 million worth of fake Modernist paintings sold by Knoedler Gallery; a messy breakup between art advisers to the stars; a wrongful-termination suit brought by the former director of the Philadelphia Museum of Art; and a fight over the legacy of Robert Indiana, the late artist who created the famous “LOVE” sculpture. In April, Nikas secured a $102.2 million jury verdict for his client, Indiana’s former business partner, after an eight-year-long dispute with an art publisher over who controls the late artist’s legacy and can profit off his work. The more litigious the art world becomes, the busier Nikas gets.

entries.title: Vanessa Horabuena
entries.author: Belinda Luscombe
paragraphs: While most artists build their careers through exhibitions at museums and galleries, Vanessa Horabuena, 41, has taken an alternative path in a parallel art world. Described by President Donald Trump as “one of the greatest artists anywhere,” Horabuena is a leading speed painter, an updated version of the vaudevillian performer known as a “lightning artist.” The act has more recently grown in popularity at beauty pageants, tourist spots, and halftime shows, but Horabuena saves it mostly for worship venues. Speed painters create large portraits of religious figures, celebrities, or bystanders in just a few minutes. Horabuena—whose 10-minute painting of Jesus was sold at a charity auction for $2.75 million on New Year’s Eve, and who boasts more than 1 million followers on TikTok—often paints to Christian music. She was a featured performer at Trump’s 2025 inauguration—and two of her paintings are reportedly hanging in the White House.

entries.author: Julie Davich
paragraphs: In the past few years, a 100-year-old artistic movement—Surrealism—has become one of the hottest topics in the art world, with a wave of exhibitions celebrating its history and a growing number of contemporary painters finding inspiration in its dreamlike aesthetic. Some of this buzz is due to the scholarship of Matthew Affron, the Philadelphia Museum of Art’s modern art curator. He co-curated the international touring exhibition “Dreamworld: Surrealism at 100,” which concluded its two-year run in Philadelphia in February, and also wrote the accompanying catalogue. The show expanded the roster of artists usually associated with the movement to include women like Leonora Carrington and Remedios Varo. “We think about ways of telling these stories for a new generation,” Affron says. In October, PMA will open the second and final installment of the first Marcel Duchamp retrospective in the U.S. in more than 50 years, organized in collaboration with MOMA. “Whether it’s the great story of Surrealism, or the career of Duchamp,” he says, “we’re looking at them from new angles.”

entries.title: Alicia Keys and Swizz Beatz Turned Collecting Art Into a Mission
entries.author: Erin McMullen
paragraphs: When Alicia Keys and Kaseem “Swizz Beatz” Dean first started collecting art together well over a decade ago, they were mostly just doing it for the love of the game. “We started collecting without a mission, to be honest,” Dean says. “We were collecting because we love art. We were collecting because it was something amazing to do together.”

Now, more than 130 pieces from the married couple’s personal trove—which they refer to as the Dean Collection—are being shown in museums across the U.S. in a traveling exhibition called “Giants.” As the name suggests, the featured works loom large, both literally and figuratively: a hulking tire wrapped in chains by Arthur Jafa, a painted diptych of BMX bike riders popping wheelies by Amy Sherald, vibrant photography from the streets of New York City shot by Jamel Shabazz. The selected works make up only a small fraction of the thousand-plus holdings the couple has acquired over time.

Since opening at the Brooklyn Museum in 2024, “Giants” has made stops in four other American cities, with still more planned across the globe through 2031. The show broke attendance records at the Museum of Contemporary Art San Diego in August by attracting more than 25,000 people in the almost four months it was there.

Keys, 45, and Dean, 48, are towering figures themselves. She is a 17-time Grammy-winning singer-songwriter; he is a DJ, rapper, and producer with a Grammy of his own. All things considered, it’s not much of a surprise that the pair has become so deeply immersed in the art world. As Dean says, “Art and music are brothers and sisters.”

It was the connection between these two creative universes that allowed the couple to zero in on a mission for the Dean Collection: they would use it to celebrate and uplift living visual artists, especially those who are Black, by creating a collection that felt like a family. Keys and Dean began to develop deeper relationships with the artists whose work they were collecting. They visited studios and brought their five children along; they answered late-night phone calls; they offered advice when they could.

“What got us a lot of love and credibility was being human and not transactional,” says Dean. Throughout the time they have been collecting, Keys says, “We’ve been able to develop a relationship with the artist that’s really from a pure place, and there’s really a friendship there. There’s a mutual respect.”
“We’ve always been in a different state of mind just because we are also artists,” she adds. “So the way we relate to artists is going to naturally be different than anybody else.”

Their shared music knowledge has also allowed Keys and Dean to bring fresh perspectives to the business side of art. Visual artists do not typically receive royalties, at least in the U.S., when their work is resold through an auction house, gallery, or private sale. If a collector buys a painting for $10,000 and sells it for $1 million one year later, the artist never sees a penny of the windfall.

“We never could understand that,” Dean says. Musicians typically receive royalties anytime their work is reproduced or used commercially. “Why should the rules apply for us and not for the visual artists?”

On Sept. 9, the couple announced Deans’ Choice—a groundbreaking elective program through Bonhams auction house that allows U.S.-based sellers to direct a percentage of proceeds to the living artist behind a sold work. Even if only a handful of sellers choose to participate, “we already won,” Dean says. “This is the beginning of something amazing, and we feel that a lot of people will do the right thing.”

Deans’ Choice was a dream that took seven years to become reality, the couple says, but their desire to do right by the artists they patronize has only grown stronger in that time. “We can’t come in and just break the rules,” Dean says. “But we could start to change things that we don’t like.”
“The ideal industry for any creative person should be a place where they are completely empowered,” Keys says. “The Dean Collection is by the artist, for the artist, with the people.”

entries.title: Rashid Johnson
entries.author: Belinda Luscombe
paragraphs: Some artists spend their lives honing their skills in one medium. Rashid Johnson’s oeuvre spans paintings, sculptures, mixed-media assemblages, mosaics, photographs, performance, films, and men’s magazine covers. It’s as if, following centuries of the stifling of Black thought, it takes a lot of avenues to explore the complexities of existence in 21st century America. “I'm not invested in medium specificity,” Johnson told TIME in 2025, on the eve of a career-defining exhibition in NYC’s Guggenheim rotunda that, after a stop in Fort Worth, Texas, will travel to his hometown of Chicago in November. He trusts his audience to follow along. “I think whoever convinced the viewer they should feel insecure… is at fault,” he says. Johnson has not taken his stratospheric art-world success lightly, using his influence to promote the work of Black artists who came before him, including McArthur Binion and Robert Colescott, as well as hosting joint exhibitions and residencies with his friends and contemporaries.

entries.title: Bernard Arnault
entries.author: Julie Davich
paragraphs: Chairman and CEO of the luxury goods conglomerate LVMH and one of the world’s richest men, Bernard Arnault has used some of his considerable fortune to build a first-rate art collection, including pieces by Francis Bacon, Jeff Koons, and Gerhard Richter. In 2014, he opened the Frank Gehry-designed Fondation Louis Vuitton in Paris, which welcomes 1.5 million visitors annually and puts on the kind of high-wattage exhibitions that only a combination of money and access can secure. In October, the museum will open a sprawling exhibition dedicated to the once-renowned, now-obscure artist, collector, and designer Gustave Fayet, bringing together Impressionist masterworks from 64 institutions and 71 private collections. As public funding for the arts in France shrinks, the foundation’s popularity exemplifies the growing influence of privately-backed art institutions in the country. Meanwhile, LVMH brands like Tiffany, Dior, and Loewe continue to bring art to new audiences by developing products and designing boutiques in collaboration with artists. A recent article estimated LVMH’s corporate art collection is worth €1 billion—and that’s not even counting Arnault’s personal holdings.

entries.title: Max Hollein
entries.author: Isa Farfan
paragraphs: As director and CEO of one of the most visited art institutions in the world, Max Hollein’s job is a novel mix of diplomat, executive, and fundraiser. The Austrian art historian took over the Metropolitan Museum of Art in 2018, at a moment when its deficit was growing and its reputation was on the rocks following the messy departure of its former director. Since his appointment, Hollein has stabilized the museum’s finances, overseen the reopening of the Rockefeller Wing for African and Oceanic art, and expanded programming for contemporary art by launching a new sculpture commission that appears on the building’s facade.

He has also attracted monumental donations, including $670 million for the construction of the Tang Wing for Modern and Contemporary Art (opening in 2030), and overseen more than 100 exhibitions, such as the largest-ever exhibit of works by Raphael in the U.S., which earned rave reviews this spring. Not all headlines have been as laudatory: in August, fashion designer John Galliano pulled out of a planned Costume Institute retrospective under pressure from donors and civic leaders. Momentum for new projects continues. Hollein’s biggest coup this year was the announcement of a merger with the nearby Neue Galerie, which will expand the museum’s holdings of 19th- and 20th-century works from Austria and Germany and see it manage the jewel-box museum founded by Ronald Lauder. Under Hollein’s watch, America’s largest art museum just keeps getting bigger.
Correction, Sept. 18
The original version of this story misstated the total donated toward construction of the Tang Wing for Modern and Contemporary Art. It is $670 million, not $550 million.

entries.title: Jenny Holzer
entries.author: Isa Farfan
paragraphs: Jenny Holzer makes art out of language. Merging sculpture and poetry, she molds and reconfigures words in ways that provoke audiences and reveal hidden truths. The Ohio-born artist broke out in the late 1970s with “Truisms” (1977–1979), a series of all-caps phrases that interrogated authority, such as “A LOT OF PROFESSIONALS ARE CRACKPOTS” and “ABUSE OF POWER COMES AS NO SURPRISE.” When she became the first woman to represent the U.S. with a solo exhibition at the Venice Biennale in 1990, she showed phrases on LED screens and carved them into a marble floor. Since then, Holzer has turned from constructing her own text to instead remixing existing writings, drawing from government archives including documentation of the Gulf War and the FBI’s redacted files on 1984 author George Orwell. Her goal remains the same: to question the mechanics of power.

This fall, the Musée d’Orsay in Paris will display Holzer’s work in an exhibition entitled “J'ai vu.” She is also planning an installation in Times Square for World AIDS Day on Dec. 1, featuring text by artists affected by the disease. Described as “radical” by artist Kiki Smith, Holzer articulates her present motivations as a “desire to be a better artist, a wish not to be a crummy person, and a desire to be of some utility to others.” As she continues to distill critical texts for the public, she finds private refuge in her pet donkey, Chicken, who lives with her in Upstate New York.

entries.title: Carmelo Anthony
entries.author: Sean Gregory
paragraphs: Athletes often draw comparisons to artists, and basketball Hall of Famer Carmelo Anthony—who danced around defenses, innovated angles, and showed a delicate touch around the basket en route to scoring 28,289 points in his 19-year NBA career—counts as a master craftsman. So it’s only fitting that Anthony, like other professional athletes, is starting to make his mark as an art collector. Anthony—who owns works from the likes of Ernie Barnes, the former pro football player who went on to become a noted painter; South African portraitist Nelson Makamo; and the urban contemporary artist Cryptik—moved out of his New York City apartment into a suburban house in 2022 to give his vast collection more breathing space.

How many pieces does he own? “I’ve stopped counting,” Anthony tells TIME. “I’m not one that goes out there to try to look for the trends, or to see what everybody else is doing. I’ve gotten more intentional on quality over quantity.”

Anthony’s love for art came early, his taste shaped by the street graffiti and Earth, Wind & Fire album covers he noticed growing up in Brooklyn and Baltimore. By the time he was drafted into the NBA in 2003, he was already familiar with Barnes, whose seminal 1976 work “The Sugar Shack,” depicting a joyous dance hall in the segregated South, had appeared on a Marvin Gaye album cover and in the credits of the 1970s hit sitcom Good Times. “How his artwork was implemented into the Black culture,” says Anthony, “was special to see.”

After Anthony joined the New York Knicks in 2011, his passion grew. He listened to former players reminisce about traversing the SoHo art scene and collecting works by the likes of Jean-Michel Basquiat and Andy Warhol. Anthony started popping into art galleries on the road, and by the time he stopped playing in 2022, he’d amassed many of the works that now fill his home.

In a busy post-NBA career (he’s also invested in wine, cannabis, apparel, and production companies), Anthony isn’t slowing down. “Everybody is looking at you crazy,” he says. “‘Melo, what are you doing?’” With art, Anthony sees endless possibilities. He may attempt, at some point, to learn painting himself. “The next step is to actually start to try to visualize stories and try it.”

One day, he’d like to bring his collection to the public. The dream location for such an opening? Baltimore, where he moved when he was 8 years old. “A lot of the art that I have comes from being emotionally attached to the city, and all things that I've been through,” says Anthony. “To be able to start it there would mean a lot.”

The collector has advice for other athletes—or anyone, really—looking to take the art plunge. “Art can be intimidating,” he says. “But just don't be in a rush. Take your time. If you don't understand it right there, leave it and come back to it. If it brings you back, then you know that's the piece. That’s when you know it's genuine.”

entries.title: Simone Leigh
entries.author: Katie White
paragraphs: “The tendency when people hear Black women’s stories is to focus on what happened to them,” Simone Leigh has said. “My work is about what they did from those compromised positions—the labor, the care, the love, the ideas.” The 58-year-old artist channels the agency, intellectual rigor, and creative accomplishments of Black women into sculpture, video art, and installation. She is best known for towering, elegant ceramic sculptures that fuse the Black female form with raffia-lined architectural silhouettes or vessels, like jugs, used throughout Africa and its diaspora. In 2022, she earned rave reviews for her solo show at the Venice Biennale, which made her the first Black woman to represent the U.S. at the exhibition. Loophole of Retreat, a recurring series she organizes, is proving just as enduring. Convening Black female thinkers, it offers new models both for gathering and documenting women’s intellectual culture. Its most recent stop? The 2022 Venice Biennale. Now, the Brooklyn-based artist is preparing for a 2027 exhibition at the Royal Academy of Arts in London. The exhibition will be her largest to date.

entries.title: Gerhard Richter
entries.author: Belinda Luscombe
paragraphs: “People won’t stop painting,” Gerhard Richter told TIME in 2012, “just as they won’t stop making music or dancing.” Five years later, Richter announced he would in fact stop painting, citing his age. But the 94-year-old continues to create, drawing in pencil every day in his studio. (“I don’t believe in God,” he told TIME. “So for me, art is a substitute.” ) Richter, who was educated both in strictly figurative techniques in former East Germany and a more expressionist style after he defected to West Germany in 1961, is revered for both his blurred photorealistic works and his abstract pieces. While several prominent artists cite Richter as an influence, his legacy is less about a particular style of painting than a set of beliefs: that realism and abstraction can coexist, and that photography can be both source and subject. As demonstrated by recent shows including a major retrospective at the Fondation Louis Vuitton in Paris, a show in New York City, and a current one in Arles, the appetite for his work hasn’t slowed. In May, one of his iconic photorealistic candle paintings sold for $35 million at auction.

entries.title: KAWS
entries.author: Naomi Rea
paragraphs: KAWS is the rare contemporary artist to command both mainstream popularity and respect from the elite art world. The 51-year-old, who rose to prominence as a graffiti writer, makes toys, paintings, and sculptures starring a moody cast of characters drawn from pop culture, like a skull-and-crossbones figure inspired by Mickey Mouse. The artist, whose real name is Brian Donnelly, has also found success across the price spectrum; his paintings have sold for up to $15 million at auction, while his $50 Uniqlo T-shirts caused stampedes in China. In September 2025, he became the retailer’s first artist in residence.

KAWS’ rabid fandom fueled his crossover to museums, which are eager to capture the attention of his 4.2 million Instagram followers. His 2026 traveling survey drew more than 163,000 people to the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art, including the most visits from children and teenagers at a show since 2019. His global domination continues this year with “KAWS: Art & Comic” at the Albertina Modern in Vienna.

entries.title: Tracey Emin
entries.author: Belinda Luscombe
paragraphs: Hiding behind the work is not Tracey Emin’s bag. Ever since she emerged alongside the bad boys of the so-called Young British Art movement in the ’90s, she has been famous for making art and conversation that equal each other in their frankness. entries.title: Thelma Golden
entries.author: Naomi Rea
paragraphs: Thelma Golden has arguably done more than anyone else to promote Black artists in the U.S. For over two decades, the director and chief curator of the Studio Museum in Harlem, founded in 1968, has forged the institution into a leading incubator and showcase for artists of African descent. And in November 2025, she made a permanent mark on New York City’s cultural landscape when the Studio Museum opened its $160 million new building on 125th Street. The 82,000-sq.-ft. facility, which looks like a charcoal-colored Jenga tower, doubled space for exhibitions and created classrooms, artist studios, and meeting spaces for community organizations. Golden started her career in the 1980s as a curator at the Whitney Museum of American Art, where she organized powerful exhibitions about Black masculinity and conceptual art that divided critics, but made her name as a fearless curator. Now, she’s focused on ensuring a long-term future for the institution she’s shaped. Alongside raising money for the new building and attracting patrons including Beyoncé, Golden created a $52 million endowment, ensuring the Studio Museum’s 9,000-work collection will be cared for well into the future.

entries.title: Michael Govan
entries.author: Taylor Dafoe
paragraphs: Michael Govan, CEO and director of the Los Angeles County Museum of Art (LACMA), has spent his career trying to redefine what a museum can be. But it’s not thought that distinguishes him. "Nothing's new in ideas," he says. "Putting them in concrete is the radical thing." It took 20 years, but that’s exactly what Govan accomplished this spring, when LACMA unveiled the David Geffen Galleries, a 347,500-sq.-ft. expansion designed by architect Peter Zumthor. The curving concrete-and-glass building has its detractors, but it is as flat and open as LA itself, embodying Govan’s commitment to deconstructing traditional hierarchies between artistic mediums and cultural geographies. Displays are organized around bodies of water, like the Pacific Ocean and Mediterranean Sea, rather than presented in a more standard chronological order, divided by country or culture. “It was really about taking the constraints off of the model and setting it free,” the 63-year-old director says. Govan, who has a reputation as a donor whisperer, has been working towards this $724 million expansion since he took the LACMA job in 2006. For him, the Geffen Galleries mark the culmination of that experience, but also the start of something new. LACMA is working to extend its collection to more communities through partnerships with schools and libraries, and is currently in the early planning stages of building a new museum in South LA. “This,” Govan declares, “is the big accessibility decade.”

entries.title: Jessica Morgan
entries.author: Julia Halperin
paragraphs: As a generation of museum directors ages out of the profession, Jessica Morgan has emerged as a museum leader who is committed to doing things differently. In July, the 57-year-old British art historian was named director of Tate, the U.K.-based organization in charge of some of the world’s most-visited art museums. She has her work cut out for her: in 2025, attendance at the Tate’s London sites remained 1.6 million short of pre-pandemic levels and workers went on strike over pay cuts.

Morgan has proven her mettle as director of the Dia Art Foundation, which operates a dozen sites across the U.S. and Germany. During her 12-year tenure, she oversaw Dia’s first acquisitions of work by African American artists and grew the number of women in the museum’s collection by more than 360%. She also demonstrated economical decision-making—like scrapping an expensive expansion of Dia’s New York City facility, and instead renovating its existing building—that is sure to serve her well in her new role.

entries.title: Matthew Bogdanos
entries.author: Tim Schneider
paragraphs: New York prosecutor Matthew Bogdanos has spent more than 20 years waging war on the black market for ancient art and objects, and the victories are piling up. As a Marine, he led the international investigation into the pillaging of the Iraq Museum in 2003. But it is the Antiquities Trafficking Unit (ATU), a division of the Manhattan district attorney’s office established by Bogdanos in 2017, that has upended the global business of looted antiquities.

Bogdanos recently estimated that the ATU has recovered around 6,350 artifacts worth nearly $500 million and repatriated nearly 6,000 of them to 38 countries. Renowned museums have been no safer from scrutiny than shadowy crime syndicates or collectors’ penthouses. To date, the ATU has reclaimed over 120 items worth more than $95 million from the Metropolitan Museum of Art alone. Suddenly, institutions and auction houses are prioritizing investments in provenance research, some antiquities sellers are avoiding New York altogether, and Bogdanos has sophisticates sweating the question that social graces and self-interest used to keep at bay: How did that artifact really get here?

entries.title: Refik Anadol
entries.author: Naomi Rea
paragraphs: What impact will AI have on art? Digital artist Refik Anadol offers an answer in the form of Dataland, the ambitious museum of AI-generated art he opened in June. The spectacular for-profit attraction in Los Angeles has been applauded for its scale (35,000 square feet) and ambition (to prove that AI can be as generative a tool for an artist as a paintbrush or a camera—an argument that’s not without controversy in the art world). The inaugural show, inspired by the Amazon rainforest, changes in real time based on visitors’ movements, as well as their biometric data, which is gathered from electronic bracelets worn in the gallery.

Anadol, 40, is among the most prominent to emerge from the pandemic-era boom for digital art. He is best known for his large-scale “data sculpture” at MOMA, an undulating wave of morphing shapes and colors he created using a custom machine-learning algorithm that mapped the museum’s collection and responded to visitors’ movements. After it debuted in 2022, the project proved so popular that its run was extended several times; it became the first generative artwork to enter the museum’s collection.

entries.title: Adriano Pedrosa
entries.author: Naomi Rea
paragraphs: The artistic director of Museu de Arte de São Paulo (MASP) in Brazil has broken out by rewriting the curator’s playbook. Pedrosa places art previously dismissed as “outsider” on equal terms with the work of academically trained artists, and eschews chronological storytelling in favor of surveys of art that play on broad themes such as “childhood” or “sexuality.” In 2025, after more than six years of planning and construction, MASP opened a $43 million tower that expanded its exhibition space by 66%. This year, Pedrosa dedicated MASP’s curatorial program to unpacking how the idea of Latin America was created and contested over time. He also defended some MASP exhibitions, including a recent show by the queer artist La Chola Poblete, from right-wing attacks. As competing political factions push fixed views of history, Pedrosa’s exhibits argue that there is no one “correct” way to view art.

entries.title: Elizabeth Alexander
entries.author: Isa Farfan
paragraphs: Cultural organizations panicked after the Trump Administration terminated a swath of arts grants in 2025, citing what it described as wasteful spending and an over-emphasis on diversity, equity, and inclusion. So Elizabeth Alexander stepped in. Through the Andrew W. Mellon Foundation, where she has served as president since 2018, Alexander created a $15 million emergency fund for state-level humanities councils affected by the rollbacks. “We don't often enough think about the arts as a crucial pillar of our democracy,” Alexander says. “Freedom of expression is one of the fundamental tenets.” A poet and scholar who performed at President Barack Obama’s 2009 inauguration, Alexander has shaped the Mellon Foundation into one of the best-funded champions of diversity in the arts. With a $7.9 billion endowment, the organization has supported ambitious initiatives such as the $500 million, multi-year Monuments Project. At a time when American history is the subject of national debate and revision, the project supports memorials to lesser-known figures and events, including monuments to Emmett Till, Mamie Till-Mobley, and Japanese Americans incarcerated during World War II.

entries.title: Larry Gagosian
entries.author: Olivia B. Waxman
paragraphs: Larry Gagosian is widely recognized as the world’s most powerful art dealer—and the only one to become a brand name. He got his start selling posters on the streets of Los Angeles in the 1970s and opened his first art gallery in 1980. Since then, he has built an empire of 19 spaces around the world and played a key role in transforming collecting from a niche pursuit into a status symbol. He now represents over 100 artists and, according to widely-cited estimates, generates more than $1 billion in annual revenue. Gagosian’s latest space—on Manhattan’s Madison Avenue—opened in April with an exhibition by the conceptual artist Marcel Duchamp. On view through Sept. 26, the show features a 1964 bicycle wheel so rare, it’s the only object of its kind not in the collection of a major museum. The 81-year-old Gagosian also regularly makes headlines on the auction floor, like in 2022 when he placed the winning $195 million bid on a 1964 Andy Warhol portrait of Marilyn Monroe at Christie’s, setting a record for the most expensive work of American art sold at auction. While he established a board of advisers nearly four years ago to help shape the gallery’s future, he has no plans to retire from his spot at the top of the art world.

entries.title: Naomi Beckwith
entries.author: Isa Farfan
paragraphs: The Chicago-born, New York-based curator Naomi Beckwith has spent her career exploring how ideas traverse borders, shaping artists around the globe rather than staying in one place. In roles at the Guggenheim Museum in New York and the Museum of Contemporary Art, Chicago, she organized exhibitions by artists of the African diaspora, including Rashid Johnson, and examined how the 1960s African American avant-garde movement informed international contemporary art.

Her latest gig brings her halfway around the world, to Kassel, Germany, where she is the artistic director for the 16th edition of Documenta. The 71-year-old festival, founded to bring international art audiences to Germany after WWII, opens next summer under Beckwith and her all-woman team. The event, which is funded by the German government, has generated controversies over its political content, direction, and hefty cost. Beckwith insists her vision will not be compromised. “I am not going to foreclose any expression from artists,” Beckwith says. “I've made that very clear in my conversations both with artists and with governments.”

entries.title: Amy Cappellazzo and Yuki Terase
entries.author: Taylor Dafoe
paragraphs: Art Intelligence Global sounds vaguely like an international spy ring. That’s not entirely a coincidence. Amy Cappellazzo and Yuki Terase spent many years handling high-profile art sales at more conventional emporia—including at Sotheby’s, where Cappellazzo was based in New York and Terase in Hong Kong—before founding their own consultancy in 2021. They’ve become instrumental art-whisperers for high-net-worth individuals, family wealth funds, artists, and elite collectors (including, this year, the estate of MOMA’s longtime board president and fairy godmother Agnes Gund), advising on acquisitions, private sales, appraisals, and long-term strategy. Rather than representing individual artists or collectors, they act as go-betweens and matchmakers, pairing buyers and sellers behind the scenes. (Before entering the art world, Terase was in the mergers and acquisitions division at Morgan Stanley’s Tokyo office.) The duo has been especially successful in integrating Western and Asian markets by zeroing in on what makes a work of art valuable to a potential collector. “I believe works of art sell best when they carry the aura of having been loved and cherished by their owners,” Cappellazzo says. “This is an X factor inherent to a work of art that is hard to assign a dollar amount to.”

entries.title: Kymberly Pinder
entries.author: Isa Farfan
paragraphs: Yale School of Art Dean Kymberly Pinder wants her Master’s of Fine Arts students to graduate debt-free. In her five years steering the most prestigious art school in the U.S., Pinder has raised $13 million towards an ambitious goal: to create what she calls an “ethical MFA” program that would ensure students don’t have to go into debt to pursue their art education, and can continue their practices after graduation without enormous loan repayments. Pinder says she hopes to nurture the “compulsion artists [have] to make work to help themselves understand how they're living in the world, and to help other people.”

Pinder, an eminent scholar of race and public art, is keenly aware of the realities facing working artists, and has endeavored to make sure students are prepared, pioneering financial literacy and grant-writing curricula at Yale and embedding students in the broader New Haven art community. Under her leadership, the school converted an underutilized Yale-owned space into a student-run gallery that highlights local artists and led art projects in a local women’s prison. This spring, Pinder was reappointed as dean for a second five-year term, giving her more time to fully realize her dream of making a top MFA program debt-free for those who need it.

entries.title: Susan Freedman
entries.author: Sarah Cascone
paragraphs: For 40 years, Susan Freedman has dedicated her life to embedding public art in the streets of New York City, pulling off ambitious, high-profile art installations by some of the world’s most visionary artists. As the president of Public Art Fund, the nonprofit founded by her mother, Doris Freedman, nearly half a century ago, she has become adept at navigating the web of government bureaucracy, leveraging her dense network of relationships to fundraise, cut through red tape, and make the extraordinary possible. “That's really how I spend my time, bringing the right people together to realize our projects,” Freedman says. Recent installations include “Between Tides,” an interactive display of artist-designed ping-pong tables on Rockaway Beach, and playful bronze sculptures of birds by Genesis Belanger installed inside the fountain in City Hall Park. Next up, Public Art Fund will unveil a permanent public art display featuring work by 19 artists in JFK Terminal 6, a follow-up to the organization’s work at LaGuardia Airport and Newark Liberty International Airport. Freedman is making sure that, even on their way out of town, people get to experience art.
Correction, Sept. 17
The original version of this story misstated Freedman's role at the Public Art Fund. She is the president, not the director.

entries.title: Joe Hage
entries.author: Naomi Rea
paragraphs: Joe Hage is the most powerful man you’ve never heard of in the art world. An accountant turned commercial lawyer, his interest in art began as that of a collector who became passionate about using his talents to help artists become more entrepreneurial. Since the early 2000s, he has been managing the careers of the world’s wealthiest and most famous artists, including Damien Hirst and Peter Doig. More like a Hollywood agent than a traditional art dealer, Hage isn’t focused on selling art to collectors as much as shaping an artist’s career by, for example, advising them on sponsorship deals, partnerships, and contracts with galleries. Alongside his careers as an artist manager and litigation advisor specializing in commercial disputes for some of the world’s biggest businesses, he has also built Heni, an international art services company that works with leading artists (including Gerhard Richter) and estates (including that of Francis Bacon) to produce prints, digital art, films, and research. Notoriously discreet, Hage stepped into the spotlight this summer when his firm, Joseph Hage Aaronson & Bremen, sponsored a major Barbara Hepworth exhibition at London’s Courtauld Gallery. As more artists look for ways to support themselves beyond the traditional gallery sales model, Hage’s tradition-bucking activities offer a blueprint at the highest level.

entries.title: Diya Vij Wants New York to Fight for Its Artists
entries.author: Isa Farfan
paragraphs: What do artists need to survive—and dream big? These questions guide the work of curator and arts administrator Diya Vij, who has spent years supporting contemporary artists at New York City institutions including the nonprofit Creative Time, where she commissioned public art and launched a fellowship for politically engaged artists.

Now, Vij is working to build arts infrastructure that can sustain artists on a much larger scale as the new commissioner of New York City’s department of cultural affairs (DCLA). Since Mayor Zohran Mamdani appointed her to steer the department in February, Vij—the first South Asian person to lead DCLA—has carved out a space for artists in the administration’s broader affordability agenda. She says she envisions a New York City that nurtures artists from their first art classes to the “big stages and all the places in between.”

This goal appears harder than ever. entries.title: Jeffrey Gibson
entries.author: Tim Schneider
paragraphs: Jeffrey Gibson’s paintings, sculptures, textiles, and performances joyfully foreground groups long marginalized in American life and history, particularly Native and queer people. In 2024, Gibson, a member of the Mississippi Band of Choctaw Indians and of Cherokee descent, became the first Indigenous American artist to represent the U.S. at the Venice Biennale, the world’s most prestigious international exhibition, with a solo presentation. His signature aesthetic fuses kaleidoscopic colors, geometric patterns, and text sampled from sources as diverse as pop music, protest mantras, and historical documents. Gibson’s larger-than-life animal sculptures enlivened the facade of the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York City for nine months in 2025 and 2026. He also unveiled Yet With a Steady Beat, an installation featuring images of traditional hand drums inscribed with slogans inspired by civil rights movements, at the Obama Presidential Center in June. In Gibson’s brilliantly colored world, resistance looks irresistible.

entries.title: Lorna Simpson
entries.author: Katie White
paragraphs: For over 30 years, Lorna Simpson has raised provocative questions about the nature of perception and how forces like racism and sexism shape our ways of seeing. Simpson rose to prominence in the early 1990s with large-scale installations featuring black-and-white photographs of Black women with their faces turned away from the viewer, paired with poetic texts that question the viewer’s assumptions. She has sought inspiration from archival imagery, plumbing vintage issues of Ebony and Jet magazines, and the Library of Congress, to create sculptures and collages that explore the legacy of America’s visual culture. She’s also contributed to that long legacy, as with a 2021 photo-collage of pop star Rihanna for the cover of Essence magazine. Now 66, Simpson has pushed herself in new directions over the last decade by embracing painting. Since 2025, her compositions—which meld imagery of melting icebergs and the female body with swirling passages of blue—have traveled from the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York City to the Punta della Dogana in Venice. “Blue is through all cultures, and possesses a poignant and amazing gravitational pull,” Simpson has said. In October, she will present a new body of work at Hauser and Wirth London.

entries.title: Banksy
entries.author: Isa Farfan
paragraphs: Street artist Banksy has publicly interrogated pressing issues ranging from immigration to war to government corruption for decades—all while denouncing the commercialized art world. Among the artist’s most recognized works are his 2003 West Bank stencil Love is in the Air, portraying a masked man hurling a flower bouquet; a series of murals drawing attention to destruction in Ukraine; and a painting that shredded itself during a Sotheby’s auction in 2018. The stunt only made it more valuable: the same work sold for a record-breaking $25.4 million in 2021.

Though the artist has long operated anonymously and under a pseudonym, a Reuters investigation published in March claimed to unmask him as a Bristol native named Robin Gunningham. The apparent exposure did not slow him down: less than two months later, Banksy unveiled a sculpture in London featuring a man walking forward, his head obscured by a flag he holds high. It also didn’t puncture his market—in May, a painting of his sold for $18 million at auction.

The photographer Steve Lazarides, who says he worked with Banksy from 1997 to 2008, condemned the recent efforts to uncover his identity. “Everyone's created an image of their own folk hero … why would you want to take that away?” Lazarides says. Today, he—and many others—regard Banksy as the world’s biggest “publicly-appointed artist” and art’s Robin Hood.

entries.title: Sheila Hicks
entries.author: Julia Halperin
paragraphs: Curators and collectors once considered artists who worked with fiber and thread less important than those who worked in marble or bronze. Not anymore. American-born, Paris-based Sheila Hicks has been a driving force behind a shift that’s moved fiber art from the periphery to the center of the contemporary art world in the past decade. Now 92, she has been committed to the form since the 1960s, creating works ranging from diminutive geometric weavings to mountains of multicolored yarn that reveal the expressive potential of the material. Having studied fiber for decades with artisans from Mexico to Morocco, she has shown how the same material can be used to create an exuberant waterfall unfurling from the ceiling and a taut experiment in warp and weft the size of a paperback book. Her work continues to find new audiences around the world, with shows in 2026 at the West Bund Museum in Shanghai; the Palais des Beaux-Arts in Lille, France; and the Instituto Tomie Ohtake in São Paulo. She is also developing a site-specific installation for the Guggenheim Abu Dhabi, scheduled to open in December. Beyond the gallery, Hicks collaborated with Dior’s artistic director Jonathan Anderson in fall 2025 to reimagine the brand’s famous Lady Dior bag in her trademark tassels.

entries.title: David Hammons
entries.author: Tim Schneider
paragraphs: David Hammons has a mythical status in the art world. For more than 60 years, he has leveraged the symbols, metaphors, and artifacts of Black life, like African masks and barbershop clippings, to create indelible sculpture and performance. The artist’s most radical project, however, has been to make dealers, institutions, and collectors abandon their rules to play by his—and adore him for it. Major museums have clamored to spotlight Hammons for decades, yet the last institutional solo show he authorized opened in 1990. His largest exhibition to date took place at the mega-gallery Hauser & Wirth in 2019, but he has declined ongoing representation. This summer, the international gallery White Cube featured him in a two-person show in New York, reflecting on his kinship with Italian artist Jannis Kounellis in the 1990s; unsurprisingly, Hammons was not formally involved. Yet his almost ironclad refusal to grant interviews or attend art events has only magnified his influence. Particularly for younger generations of Black artists grappling with how to navigate the art world’s growing demands, Hammons offers an alternative vision—that success can come without compromise.

entries.title: Emily Wei Rales
entries.author: Belinda Luscombe
paragraphs: A crowded gallery with a buzzy show has its charms, but Emily Wei Rales and her ex-husband, the billionaire industrialist Mitch Rales, wanted a different way to display their impressive modern and contemporary art collection. Glenstone, where the Taiwanese-Canadian Wei Rales is director and co-founder, differs in key ways from most galleries, private or public. Its 300 acres offer space for contemplating nature alongside art, it’s in suburban Maryland rather than a city center, and its gallery guides are instructed to ask questions rather than answer them. (To keep the vibe contemplative, children under 12 cannot attend during regular hours.) “We try to make sure that there are no barriers to letting people stay as long as they want in front of an artwork,” says Wei Rales, who got her start working at New York galleries. The museum is free and guests who arrive by public bus don’t even have to book. The Pavillions, its main building, reopened in 2025 after an 18-month closure for repairs, with exhibitions of work by Alex Da Corte, Jenny Holzer, Charles Ray, and Jaune Quick-to-See-Smith. Wei Rales says that prioritizing the viewer’s experience is key, even though the approach initially confused observers who suspected Glenstone was either a vanity project or a tax write-off. “It took us every bit of 10 years to convince people that we weren't just a flash in the pan,” she says.
