entries.title: Gabriel Orozco
entries.author: Kate Brown
paragraphs: Few artists of Gabriel Orozco's stature have given up a permanent studio. Yet for three decades, the pioneering Mexican artist, who has made a career out of turning the everyday into the extraordinary, has let commissions and exhibitions define where he lives and how he works. Orozco's pieces are subtle yet monumental: an oval-shaped billiards table, a carefully-organized array of debris left behind on a sports field, a Citroën car reduced to two-thirds of its normal width. “To keep making art, you have to put yourself in the position of a beginner,” he has said. “You have to be excited by a stone on the sidewalk or, like a child, the flight of a bird.”

Orozco’s materials are as wide-ranging as the places he calls home. Over the past decade, he has designed three sculptural landscapes, including 800 acres in Chapultepec Park in Mexico City, and a garden that opened April 3 at Seoul's Leeum Museum, with 10 circular plazas radiating from a central point. (The nomadic artist will open a solo show of work at the museum in February.) This summer, he also branched into photography with Public Nature, an art project installed on 300 bus shelters in New York City, Chicago, and Boston from July through September. Across a dozen different images, nature seemed to swallow urban spaces: vines overtook pipes and a tree's roots appeared to spill onto the sidewalk below.

entries.title: Ronald Lauder
entries.author: Belinda Luscombe
paragraphs: For significant art collectors who want to display some of their works to the public in perpetuity, there are not a lot of options: they can start their own art museum or they can donate to an existing institution. Billionaire Ronald Lauder has now done both. He founded the Neue Galerie in 2001 to showcase his treasury of 20th century Austrian and German art, most famously Gustav Klimt’s 1907 Portrait of Adele Bloch-Bauer (better known as The Lady in Gold). In May, he surprised the art world by announcing plans to merge the Neue with the Metropolitan Museum of Art just up Fifth Avenue in New York City, offering a model for how a private museum can survive several generations while maintaining its distinct character. The cosmetics heir and his daughter Aerin are planning to kick-start a $200 million endowment and to donate 13 works that are not already in the newly formed Met Ronald S. Lauder Neue Galerie to help ensure its longevity.

entries.title: Theaster Gates
entries.author: Taylor Dafoe
paragraphs: Theaster Gates is modelling how artists can help build and preserve civic infrastructure. Fusing his background in Japanese ceramics and urban planning, Gates’ work has used art, food, and music to inspire moments of community engagement and cultural exchange. In 2010, he founded the Rebuild Foundation, a nonprofit that transforms buildings in under-resourced, historically Black neighborhoods across Chicago’s South Side into hubs for gathering and performance. The foundation’s newest project, an abandoned elementary school-turned-art space called the Land School, opened last September, around the same time the University of Chicago’s Smart Museum of Art staged Gates’ first institutional show in his hometown. Since then, the artist has presented a show at Gagosian that celebrated the life and work of the enslaved ceramicist David Drake; debuted a permanent installation at the new Obama Presidential Center; organized an exhibition of Japanese art for Prada; and earned a Guggenheim Fellowship.

entries.title: Florentina Holzinger
entries.author: Belinda Luscombe
paragraphs: Standing out at the Venice Biennale, an art festival known for provocation, requires a strong commitment to causing a stir. This year, the Austrian choreographer-performance artist Florentina Holzinger did just that. For her piece Seaworld Venice, she had naked women drive jet skis in circles for hours, naked women scuba dive in a tank of water that was being fed by two urinals (via a NASA-grade filtration system), naked women climbing a rotating weather vane and, finally, naked women using their bodies as the clapper in an enormous bell. (Often, Holzinger herself took on that particularly demanding role.) In a city full of water and historic painted images of the nude female form, visitors waited in snaking lines for the chance to see what all the fuss was about. Holzinger, 40, has also made works featuring roller skating nuns and live body modification. Having initially set out to be a dancer, Holzinger is taking art to a new and yet familiar artistic medium: the human body.
Correction, Sept. 18

entries.title: El Anatsui
entries.author: Belinda Luscombe
paragraphs: El Anatsui is that very rare artist whose work transcends continental cultural boundaries. In 2024, he had works unveiled in 20 cities as far-flung geographically and culturally as Shanghai, London, Dubai, and Lagos. And the 82-year old Ghanaian artist’s popularity is particularly robust in the U.S., where one of his quilt-like works went for $2.2 million at New York’s Frieze art fair in May. El, as he likes to be called, is most famous for his colossal wall hangings made of tiny, linked-up pieces of metal, which on closer inspection turn out to be the screw tops or neck sleeves of bottles of alcohol or other drinks. Anatsui has often referred to the cycle of trade that brought so many of the caps to his environment: Africans were taken by force through Ghana to labor on the U.S. plantations to produce sugar and rum that was shipped to Europe, then sent to Africa. “The drink represented here by bottle caps links all three continents,” he has noted. The esteem in which his work is held now joins them in another way.

entries.title: Josh Kline
entries.author: Julia Halperin
paragraphs: Josh Kline has managed to build a celebrated career by making astute art about class, a subject most people would prefer not to talk about. entries.title: Hito Steyerl
entries.author: Kate Brown
paragraphs: Hito Steyerl is not afraid of taking on the specter of Big Tech. The German artist, theorist, author, and professor creates videos that investigate how digital systems reshape politics, labor, and what it means to be human. Some of Steyerl’s most influential contributions have also been on the page, in books like The Wretched of the Screen, where she has written about the collapse of images into near-worthlessness in the internet age. "She reveals the ghosts in the machine, and the reality that appears to be smooth and fast and high definition is shown as granular, physical, social, and politically constructed," says Massimiliano Gioni, the director of the New Museum in New York City. Steyerl’s latest film, Mechanical Kurds (2025), on view at the New Museum, examines outsourced digital labor in Kurdistan, where refugees train facial-recognition AI systems. The film won her the European Commission’s the S+T+ARTS Prize in June, an annual award for projects straddling science, technology, and art. For a rising generation of artists looking to contend with seemingly overwhelming challenges, ranging from AI to climate catastrophe, in their work, “she is the godmother,” says Chiara Costa, head of programs at Fondazione Prada, where Steyerl’s “The Island” is on view until October.

entries.title: Catherine Opie
entries.author: Taylor Dafoe
paragraphs: Catherine Opie’s recent survey at London’s National Portrait Gallery opened with a picture of the artist at 9 years old, flexing her muscles like goalposts. It was an early example of what would become a lifelong project, probing the formation and performance of identity through pictures. The photographer’s portraits of LGBTQIA+ people—alternately intimate, empowering, and playful—have long made her a queer icon, but now Opie is leaning into her role as a generational mentor. “I wanted to be there on the ground at the time when people were feeling vulnerable and harmed again,” she says of the five shows she opened last year, all of which she co-curated. “It's really important for me to hold a place of optimism within activism.” Opie, who recently retired from a 32-year tenure teaching at UCLA, is now dividing her time among several projects, including a film in which she plays a character called Lesbian Cowboy. The artist shared a sketch of the figure with a group of museum workers earlier this year; she says seven of them swiftly got tattoos of it.

entries.title: Salman Toor
entries.author: Taylor Dafoe
paragraphs: Liberation and loneliness are two sides of the same coin in the work of Pakistani American Salman Toor, 42, who paints young brown men in states of convergence and of isolation. Sometimes, the men are dancing at a bar, bathed in emerald light; other times, they are alone, lying in bed. These scenes recall Toor’s early experience of, in his words, "coming out through painting" and reconciling with the fallout. "There were repercussions for me because I straddle two cultures," he says, noting that back in his home country, where homosexuality is illegal, “there was a sense of shock and betrayal.” Toor’s prominence in a growing movement to depict queer intimacy on canvas has endeared him to curators and collectors. In the years since his breakthrough show at the Whitney in 2020, he has seen his paintings sold at auction for more than $1 million, toured a solo exhibition to four museums, participated in the Venice Biennale, and sold out a two-part gallery show. His first solo European exhibition will open at the Courtauld Gallery in London in October.

entries.title: Amalia Mesa-Bains
entries.author: Sarah Cascone
paragraphs: The daughter of undocumented Mexican immigrants to the U.S., Amalia Mesa-Bains, 83, has dedicated her career to celebrating Chicano culture, both as an artist and educator. Her installations are based on altars, specifically the Día de los Muertos displays known as ofrendas, and incorporate talismanic personal effects. She coined the term domesticana for her own brand of Latina working-class feminism, which brings into the domestic sphere the historically male-dominated concept of rasquachismo, or making the most with the least. A late-career retrospective, which toured the country from 2023 to 2025, brought the MacArthur fellow’s practice to a wider audience—and watching the way people connected to her art changed her own understanding of her work, she says, as she saw the universality in its themes of ancestry and memory, illness and healing. “What I'm aiming at begins within my own narrative, but it’s broad enough that many people find themselves in it,” Mesa-Bains says. Looking ahead, her work will be included in “World Making,” a 2027 group show at Tufts University in Medford, Mass., featuring recent fellowship recipients from the U.S. Latinx Art Forum.

entries.title: Magdalene Odundo
entries.author: Naomi Rea
paragraphs: As a younger generation of artists embraces ceramics as an artistic medium, many are looking to the work of 76-year-old Magdalene Odundo for inspiration. The Kenyan-born British potter makes vessels by hand, burnishing them so highly, they look as if they are lit from within.

Since the 1990s, Odundo’s work has been collected by top institutions including the Metropolitan Museum of Art and the British Museum. More recently, her market has grown substantially as tastemakers fire up enthusiasm for contemporary ceramics. Her auction record, set in 2025, is nearly $1 million. Artists including Theaster Gates have cited her influence, and Dior creative director Jonathan Anderson used her curvilinear forms as a starting point for a line of sculptural accessories at his couture debut in January. Still pushing her own boundaries, Odundo recently experimented with a new medium, glass, for her debut exhibition with the prominent gallery Xavier Hufkens in Brussels in November 2025.

entries.title: Komal Shah
entries.author: Julie Davich
paragraphs: After a career at the highest levels of the male-dominated tech industry, Komal Shah left the field for a new challenge: advocating for the work of contemporary female artists. In less than a decade, the India-born, Silicon Valley-based collector has assembled more than 400 colorful, brawny, largely abstract paintings, sculptures, and textiles made by women. An exhibition of her collection has been traveling museums around the U.S. since 2023, with two more stops to come in Indiana and Arizona. Some of her treasures include the last known painting ever made by abstract expressionist Joan Mitchell and a canvas by the American artist Janet Sobel, who pioneered drip painting before Jackson Pollock became famous for it. While the show, “Making Their Mark,” was on view at the National Museum of Women in the Arts in Washington, D.C., in March, Shah hosted a forum for 350 art professionals to address the gender disparity in “recognition, valuation, and perception” across the art world, as she said in her opening remarks. Next spring, she’s hosting a more localized version of the event to coincide with the show’s six-month residency at the Indianapolis Museum of Art.

entries.title: Michael Heizer
entries.author: Isa Farfan
paragraphs: For Michael Heizer, art is not simply a two-dimensional painting displayed on a wall. Instead, it’s closer to architecture: monumental constructions and engravings into the land that people can walk around and explore. Born to an archaeological anthropologist father, Heizer naturally took to excavation as the subject of his art and to natural terrain as his canvas. In 2022, the 81-year-old finished City, a 1½-mile-long by ½-mile-wide complex of earth and concrete forms in the Nevada desert, which he began building in 1970. “He is an innovator of this idea of a monumental negative as being powerful,” says Michael Govan, the CEO of the Los Angeles County Museum of Art, who has worked with Heizer since the 1990s. “A lot of his work actually is about displacement. He digs a hole, and then he puts something else in it; he digs a hole and makes a mound negative next to it.” City may be complete, but Heizer isn’t resting on his laurels. This spring, he installed two sprawling sculptures—which look like elegantly curving lines carved into the gallery floor—at Gagosian in New York City.

entries.title: Philomene Magers and Monika Sprüth
entries.author: Julie Davich
paragraphs: Without gallerists Monika Sprüth and Philomene Magers, European collectors might not have been exposed to the work of boundary-pushing American artists like Cindy Sherman, Barbara Kruger, or Jenny Holzer. The German dealers have long championed politically-engaged female artists and played an important role in making the German art market considerably less male-dominated than it was when they were starting out. From their humble origins in Cologne, Germany, the duo operates galleries in Berlin, London, Los Angeles, and New York, working with 80 international artists and estates. Their Los Angeles location, across the street from the Los Angeles County Museum of Art, celebrated its 10th anniversary earlier this year with a sprawling show that featured 90 works by 59 artists and spilled over from the white-cube gallery into the vacant dining area of a former Sizzler restaurant down the street. (The dealers even installed monitors to show video art at individual booths.) Sprüth Magers is among the few female-led galleries operating at a global scale—and they’ve maintained relationships with their core artists since the gallery’s founding over 40 years ago.

entries.title: Sarah Lewis
entries.author: Sarah Cascone
paragraphs: In her quest to ensure recognition for the contributions of Black artists, Sarah Lewis wears many hats. She is a professor at Harvard University, where her course “Vision and Justice” is the second-most popular in the core curriculum. She is also an author, currently adapting the course into a book of the same name, due out in late 2027. And she is the curator of “If Emmett Till lived,” a new exhibition at the Museum of Contemporary Photography at Columbia College Chicago featuring work by 110 artists imagining a world where the 1955 lynching of the 14-year-old never took place. The show includes photos that track what his untaken journey home from Mississippi to Chicago might have looked like and explores the years Till missed. Lewis’ work interrogates how looking at images, like the historic photographs of Till’s mutilated body, can lead to social change, as pictures force the public to confront racial injustice in a visceral way. Next up, she’ll appear in Ava DuVernay’s documentary 14th, about the 14th Amendment to the U.S. Constitution, which granted citizenship to all people born in the country.

entries.title: Annabelle Selldorf
entries.author: Julia Halperin
paragraphs: If the art world has an unofficial architect, it’s Annabelle Selldorf. The German-born founder of Selldorf Architects received rave reviews for her understated, elegant renovation of the Frick Collection in New York City, which cost $220 million and opened in April 2025 after a five-year closure. The project involved building a 220-seat auditorium beneath a tranquil garden and surgically transforming the Frick family’s former bedrooms into publicly accessible galleries. It cemented Selldorf’s reputation as the anti-starchitect: her minimalist style allows her to untangle existing problems with beloved buildings and let the art take center stage. Now, she’s taking on a fresh, high-profile commission. Her firm was chosen for the more than $315 million redesign of the Grande Colonnade of the Louvre in Paris—the museum’s largest renovation in 40 years. Meanwhile, Selldorf remains the architect art dealers like David Zwirner have on speed dial to renovate their offices and design their galleries around the world.

entries.title: Maxwell Graham
entries.author: Julie Davich
paragraphs: Many headlines about the art market in the past year have focused on the challenges facing small and midsize galleries in an increasingly winner-takes-all art market. New York gallerist Maxwell Graham is bucking that trend. Since 2011, the dealer has managed to thrive while presenting challenging conceptual art by the likes of Cameron Rowland and Tiffany Sia. “I have found that private patrons find the complexity of these artists’ work to be enriching to engage with and live with,” Graham says. Last year New York magazine art critic Jerry Saltz anointed his exhibition—titled “This artwork did not sell” and featuring works, as the name suggests, that failed to find buyers in earlier shows—as one of the best of 2025. Now, Graham is exploring what it looks like to grow sustainably. On Sept. 9, he moved from the Lower East Side to a fifth-floor, 6,000-sq.-ft. space in the gallery hub of Tribeca. He also recently secured representation of the photographer Zoe Leonard, who previously showed with the much deeper-pocketed gallery Hauser & Wirth. “I have tried to let artists determine the art, the exhibitions, even the overall vision of the gallery,” Graham says, “and if the gallery has functioned at all, it is because the artists are visionaries.”

entries.title: Maurizio Cattelan Is On a Mission to Shake Us From Complacency
entries.author: Naomi Rea
paragraphs: Few have mastered the art of going viral better than Maurizio Cattelan. The Italian artist has made headlines for subversive conceptual works that infuriate the masses and sell for eye-popping prices. Highlights include a life-size depiction of Pope John Paul II being struck down by a meteorite (which sold at auction for $2.7 million in 2004) and a fully functional gold toilet called America (Ripley’s Believe It or Not! bought a version for $12.1 million in November). One of his most famous provocations, a banana duct-taped to a wall that last sold for a cool $6.2 million at auction, is on view at the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum’s exhibition “Pop: 1960 to Now,” in New York City.

Having grown up in Padua, Italy, in a working-class family, Cattelan entered the art world without formal training. He attributes his nose for inciting conversation—and debate—to his outsider background. His perspective is a “bridge between the elite world and the normal world,” he says.

He imbues his sculptures with humor and surprise designed to spark conversations about serious themes, including mortality and contemporary systems of value and social order—“insanities,” he says, that haunt him. Cattelan’s works have been called sacrilegious, but he insists the shock factor of his work is overblown: “Reality is always more provoking than what I do.”

Cattelan announced his retirement from artmaking after a Guggenheim retrospective in 2011. That lasted only five years, but it wasn’t until 2024 that he returned to traditional gallery exhibitions, with a show at Gagosian that included 17-ft.-tall gold-plated panels, pockmarked with holes: in a commentary on guns in America, he hired licensed marksmen to fire more than 20,000 rounds of ammunition into the panels. “I only recently started to feel like an artist,” he says. “It’s as if suddenly I had a maturity that probably other artists had out of school or always had.”

The epiphany comes just in time. In September, following Cattelan’s win of the 2026 Preis der National-galerie, Germany’s top contemporary art prize, Berlin’s Neue Nationalgalerie opened his biggest show in years. Uninterested in putting together a “greatest hits” compilation, Cattelan insists the show is not a retrospective. The exhibition, titled “Night,” invokes the events of German history to probe universal concepts of power, defeat, life, and death. It features transgressive new commissions including Dust, a fire extinguisher that, in accordance with the deceased’s wishes, contains the ashes of a friend of Cattelan’s, and Purgatory, a site-specific reconstruction of the Brandenburg Gate. These are shown alongside conversation-starting historical works like Cattelan’s diminutive 2001 sculpture of Adolf Hitler on his knees in prayer, as if asking for forgiveness, which takes on heightened meaning in Berlin.

With shows forthcoming in Mexico City, Buenos Aires, and Sydney, Cattelan no longer sees retirement in the cards. Instead, he will continue his mission to shake both himself and his audience from complacency. And as he turns 66, he is also ready to shed the “court jester” moniker that has dogged his career. The forthcoming Berlin exhibition, he says, “is a show that will finally demonstrate that the label someone gave me some years ago might be excessive and that there is some seriousness and depth in what I do.”

entries.title: Lauren Halsey
entries.author: Naomi Rea
paragraphs: One of the most successful artists of her generation, Lauren Halsey has committed to funneling the art world’s largesse back into the South Central Los Angeles community that raised her. In March, her nonprofit Summaeverythang opened “sister dreamer,” an 18-month-long sculpture project celebrating the neighborhood. The initiative will stay in the area, moving into a permanent home—featuring classrooms, an art gallery, and an outdoor sculpture garden and sports court—in 2028.

Halsey’s sculptures take inspiration from all forms of Black cultural expression, melding styles including ancient Egypt and Afrofuturism. Her 10-ft.-long reclining sphinx and wall relief depicting local community members as ancient deities presides over the Egyptian galleries at the newly expanded Los Angeles County Museum of Art. Having shown in some of art’s most august spaces, including the Venice Biennale and the Metropolitan Museum of Art, Halsey is one of a growing cohort of millennial artists using the establishment’s validation to build cultural institutions outside the art-world system.

entries.title: Trevor Paglen
entries.author: Isa Farfan
paragraphs: Trevor Paglen is part detective, part hacker, and part poet. Raised in a military family and holding degrees in the seemingly disparate fields of art, geology, comparative religion, and music composition, the highly decorated artist is fascinated by the way mass surveillance and artificial intelligence shape perception. In March, Paglen added the LG Guggenheim Award, a $100,000 unrestricted cash prize, to his list of accolades, which includes a 2017 MacArthur “Genius” grant. He has launched a diamond-shaped satellite into space, photographed secret prisons and military bases, and made a cube-shaped sculpture out of radioactive material collected from the nuclear exclusion zone in Fukushima, Japan, and the Trinity atomic bomb test site in New Mexico. Paglen says the cube will be viewable to the public in up to 30,000 years when he estimates the Fukushima exclusion zone, where it’s held, is deemed safe. This year, Paglen published How to See Like a Machine: Images After AI, translating his art practice into a legible conversation about image-making and surveillance in the age of AI slop. Paglen says he’s currently working on a part-science, part-art project with Cornell University neuroscientists exploring the effects of “new types of media” on the human brain.

entries.title: Alison Luchs
entries.author: Isa Farfan
paragraphs: As museums all over the world work to broaden their reach through social media, the National Gallery of Art in Washington, D.C., has broken through online with a little help from Alison Luchs, its 77-year-old curator of early European sculpture. Luchs, who previously used Instagram only to keep tabs on her grandniece and nephew, went viral last winter for using Gen-Z slang—like “chopped,” “yoinked,” and “bussin’”—to explain sophisticated 16th century European artworks. After watching Luchs give a “deadpan” gallery tour, Sydni Myers, the museum’s senior manager of social media, hatched the idea for the video series and enlisted social media producer Mary King to write scripts. Since her side-splitting short-form series, “The Museum Rizzler,” went live in December, Luchs has brought in over 32 million views to the National Gallery’s social media accounts and 175,000 new Instagram followers. Her videos also won the museum two 2026 Webby awards. Hoping that Luchs’ social media popularity translates to increased attendance, the institution plans to develop a comedic museum tour starring the curator, titled “Lore Drop.” Luchs has no plans to stop entertaining Gen Z so long as she and the team continue to low-key buss it down together.

entries.title: Christine Sun Kim
entries.author: Kate Brown
paragraphs: The California-born, Berlin-based artist Christine Sun Kim has become a defining voice of her generation by making visible society's relationship to sound—and the realities of Deafness. With humor and poignancy, Kim dismantles assumptions about hearing, language, and access through musical notation, infographics, and American Sign Language. Her charcoal series Degrees of Deaf Rage transforms geometry-class angles into everyday frustrations, from "obtuse rage" (uncaptioned videos) to "full-on rage" (museums hosting Deaf programming without employing Deaf staff). In 2020, she signed "America the Beautiful" and the national anthem in American Sign Language at the Super Bowl. A drawing she made about the experience is among nearly 100 pieces in a traveling survey exhibition at the Walker Art Center in Minneapolis that closed in August. "Deafness is a topic too few people consider or speak about," says Léon Kruijswijk, performance curator at the Mudam in Luxembourg, which will open an exhibition of Kim’s work in September. "She works against centuries of oppression and medical erasure with lyricism."

entries.title: Lawrence Abu Hamdan
entries.author: Belinda Luscombe
paragraphs: In the long and storied history of mixing art and activism, Lawrence Abu Hamdan’s work is a fascinating iteration. Abu Hamdan, 40, born in Jordan and raised in Yorkshire, England, uses sound to investigate human rights abuses and puts his findings into immersive audio-based installations, incorporating film, objects and performance. In a nod to the detective-like nature of his work, he calls himself a “private ear.” A joint winner of the 2019 Turner Prize, Abu Hamdan has interviewed former detainees at a Syrian military prison, using their recollection of the sounds of footsteps and meal hatches to create a layout of the notorious space, and conducted an audio analysis of the killing of 15 paramedics and rescue staff in Gaza. Most recently, his organization Earshot’s investigation into whether an acoustic weapon was used to break up a March 2025 protest in Belgrade, Serbia, inspired a film installation on view at the 2026 Venice Biennale. It will also be the subject of a show at London’s Barbican Centre in September.

entries.title: Anne Kraybill
entries.author: Belinda Luscombe
paragraphs: Does art really exist if nobody ever sees it? This question drives Anne Kraybill, the CEO of Art Bridges, a kind of art-sharing enterprise that helps extract works from viewer-free storage rooms so they can be displayed at museums (often rural, often under-resourced) around the U.S. The concept is more complicated than it sounds because of insurance, shipping costs, and issues around preservation—as well as the general tendency for art institutions to operate in silos. Art Bridges, with funds provided by Walmart heiress Alice Walton, helps clear obstacles to the free exchange of art, with training, logistical help, and of course, funding. Currently, for example, it’s supporting the Heckscher Museum in Huntington, N.Y., as it lends an exhibition of Emma Stebbins sculpture to the Driehaus in Chicago starting in October. One bugbear of Kraybill’s, for example, is the strict humidity standard that many galleries impose on other institutions before lending out works—standards that old, rural buildings often cannot meet. Art Bridges has found and funded research and conferences to clarify what kind of climate control is necessary to protect artworks, and what is merely optimal. Art Bridges is now working with 253 museums. “Collectively,” says Kraybill, “there's more than enough art to bring these new experiences to the public across the country.”

entries.title: Michael Armitage
entries.author: Naomi Rea
paragraphs: Kenyan British painter Michael Armitage is a leading figure among young African artists channeling their international success into building local arts infrastructure. In 2020, Armitage founded the Nairobi Contemporary Art Institute to mount exhibitions, preserve archives, and host conversations about East African artists. His own lyrical compositions draw upon and revive the region’s cultural history: he paints on an ancient local material—bark cloth—and has built a distinctive aesthetic language fusing East African and Western European visual traditions. His work often melds real-world events, like an incident of police violence in Kenya during the COVID lockdown or the country’s 2017 elections, with dreamlike landscapes and folk tales in liquid color.

In a testament to the global resonance of his work, his painting The Fourth Estate is included in a group show of contemporary British art at Nasher Museum of Art in North Carolina through July 2027. And a major solo presentation of his work, “The Promise of Change,” exhibits dozens of paintings at the Palazzo Grassi, the Venetian museum founded by the French billionaire François Pinault, through January.

entries.title: Sarah Arison
entries.author: Belinda Luscombe
paragraphs: Millennials have a reputation for being less interested in arts philanthropy, but Sarah Arison, 41, is an exception. She serves on the boards of nine non-profit arts organizations and leads two significant ones, as president of the board of the Museum of Modern Art in New York City and chair of the board of YoungArts, a Miami-based group that supports young artists at the beginning of their journeys. She comes by her philanthropic interests naturally—her grandparents, Ted and Lin Arison, founded YoungArts in 1981, having made a fortune with Carnival Cruise Lines. That organization reports having helped 24,000 young artists of all stripes, including Amanda Gorman, Timothee Chalamet, and visual artist Doug Aitken since its inception. Arison is also president of the Arison Arts Foundation, her family's private grantmaking enterprise. From these perches, she has nurtured the careers of artists from many fields at a crucial early stage. Having honed her philanthropic skills on the board of MOMA’s contemporary art outpost PS1, she also understands what emerging artists need most: creative mentorship and financial support.

entries.title: Gus Casely-Hayford
entries.author: Naomi Rea
paragraphs: How can museums win over the next generation? Ask Gus Casely-Hayford. The inaugural director of the V&A East, a branch of the London art and design museum that opened fully in April, is intent on drawing in the elusive Gen Z population. Bringing experience from previous roles in museums, education, and broadcasting, Casely-Hayford laid the groundwork by personally visiting more than 100 local schools and consulting 30,000 young people on what they wanted out of a museum. The conversations led to the Storehouse, an open-storage depot that allows visitors to view selections from the museum’s 280,000-object collection in person—and even handle them if they’re not too fragile. The facility, which opened in May 2025, drew nearly 450,000 visitors in its first year, on par with Kensington Palace. Meanwhile, the V&A East’s first exhibition, on Black British music, was shaped by an advisory group of local 16- to 25-year-olds. The museum hopes to offer proof that young people want a say in how their museums operate—as well as a peek into the back room.

entries.title: Wael Shawky
entries.author: Kate Brown
paragraphs: It's no accident that Art Basel picked the Egyptian artist Wael Shawky to serve as the inaugural artistic director of its first art fair in Qatar, and in the Middle East. One of the Arab world's leading contemporary art figures, Shawky has roots in Doha, where he heads up Fire Station, an artist residency run by Qatar Museums. At the fair in early February, he swapped traditional trade-show-style booths for curated solo presentations. The event drew around 17,000 visitors, including members of the region's royal families—a solid showing for a first-year fair.

In his own work, Shawky reimagines history through Arab perspectives, often using puppetry. At the 2024 Venice Biennale, his video installation Drama 1882—an opera about the Urabi Revolt, a late 19th century uprising in Egypt against British and French control—drew snaking lines. Since its Venice run, the work has traveled the globe, including showings in Los Angeles, Amsterdam, Sydney, and Paris. In his film I Am Hymns of the New Temples (on view at M+ in Hong Kong through October) actors reenact Mediterranean myths in the ancient city of Pompeii, exploring the universal themes that unite national stories.

entries.title: Cecilia Alemani
entries.author: Isa Farfan
paragraphs: It’s one thing to have the exhibitions you organize be scrutinized by the art world. It’s quite another to open yourself up to criticism from everyday New Yorkers (not to mention millions of tourists). But as curator of High Line Art, the only dedicated contemporary art program at a New York City park, the Milan-born Cecilia Alemani has done just that. Hosting a sculpture series situated on the elevated railway turned walkway, she’s proved that public art can be both cutting-edge and accessible. In 2024, she unveiled Iván Argote’s Dinosaur, a towering sculpture of a pigeon that became so popular that over 7,000 people signed a petition started last December protesting its replacement. The work was widely adored, Alemani says, because “many people recognized themselves” in the scrappy bird. In April, she welcomed the program’s next commission, Tuan Andrew Nguyen’s 27 ft. Bamiyan-inspired Buddha, whose hands are made from melted artillery shells from Afghanistan. Outside New York, Alemani has become a go-to biennial curator, organizing the 59th Venice Biennale in 2022 and the 12th Site Santa Fe International last year. In New Mexico, she expanded the exhibition to an unprecedented 14 offsite venues, including a local cannabis dispensary.

entries.title: Cameron Rowland
entries.author: Julia Halperin
paragraphs: Cameron Rowland’s work pushes audiences to consider how the law, the prison system, and the legacy of slavery have structured the world in ways visible and invisible. To make their point, the American artist, 37, often positions objects in a gallery or public space that seem innocuous, but are carefully chosen and situated, like five benches they quietly (and surreptitiously) placed in a New York City park to honor its unmarked Black burial grounds. Last October, Rowland’s profile rose when their work Replacement (2025)—a red, green, and black flag representing the French overseas department of Martinique, displayed in place of France’s national flag—was removed from the facade of the Palais de Tokyo in Paris. Also removed: the accompanying caption, which noted that “Black Martinicans have pursued the end of French rule for 390 years.” Museum authorities explained the commissioned work violated a rule that public institutions must maintain political neutrality. The removal brought even more attention to Rowland and their commentary, stoking a conversation about the enduring legacy of French colonialism. In November 2026, the artist will present a major solo exhibition of new work at Mumok in Vienna.

entries.title: Petra Collins
entries.author: Taylor Dafoe
paragraphs: Petra Collins was a true It Girl of the 2010s, a star on both sides of the camera. Working as a model for and protege of photographer Ryan McGinley, and as the resident photographer for Tavi Gevinson’s Rookie magazine, she introduced a visual language—an analogue blend of muted ’70s hues and ’90s teen cues—that scratched a millennial itch for life pre-cell phone. It was novel, then everywhere, including on the TV show Euphoria, which further popularized her gauzy, neon aesthetic. Now 33, Collins is still omnipresent, seen on the cover of magazines like i-d and Vogue Korea, or shooting fashion campaigns for Miu Miu and Coach. She recently released her ninth book, STAR, and filmed a music video for Olivia Rodrigo—the first such project ever shot inside the Palace of Versailles. Once associated with the Tumblr-era internet, she now straddles the worlds of fine art, fashion, and pop culture.

entries.title: Alex Da Corte
entries.author: Taylor Dafoe
paragraphs: If David Lynch designed Pee-wee’s Playhouse, it might look something like the art of Alex Da Corte. The 46-year-old’s room-sized installations brim with Benetton-colored walls, paintings, and sculptures that together conjure a feeling of what he calls jamais vu—that disorienting sensation where something very familiar suddenly seems strange and new. In Da Corte’s eyes, symbols of American culture, both mass and niche—from Big Bird to the performance artist Allan Kaprow—become mysterious and uncanny. He is best known for his films, especially ones in which he cosplays a motley cast of characters that includes Eminem, Mr. Rogers, and Frankenstein. The goal, Da Corte says, is to “invite a new interpretation of what you see and how you see.” After major showings at the Venice Biennale, the Whitney Biennial, and the Met, De Corte is looking for new challenges. He is co-curator of the Whitney Museum’s forthcoming survey of Roy Lichtenstein, whose slick pop paintings are a touchstone, and will debut a feature-length, stop-motion opera at the Buffalo AKG Art Museum in December.

entries.title: Tuan Andrew Nguyen
entries.author: Taylor Dafoe
paragraphs: Tuan Andrew Nguyen traces the ripple effects of colonialism, displacement, and war in his art. The Vietnamese-American artist is known for his poetic films and sculpture, but his work begins before he ever enters the studio or editing bay, with extensive travel and research in places ranging from Malaysia to Senegal to the Philippines. In awarding him a MacArthur “Genius” grant in 2025, the jury noted, “Nguyen recovers histories that would otherwise be lost and pieces together fragmented cultural inheritances for future generations.” His materials—including bomb remnants, archival family photographs, and singing bowls—embody his interest in examining both the legacy of violence and the potential for healing. This spring, he showed at the Venice Biennale and debuted a 27-ft. sandstone sculpture on New York City’s High Line. The work pays homage to the sixth century Bamiyan Buddhas in Afghanistan that were destroyed by the Taliban in 2001.

entries.title: Loïc Gouzer
entries.author: Julia Halperin
paragraphs: Loïc Gouzer has made a career out of shaking up the once staid and stuffy auction business. While hundreds of objects might be sold in a single afternoon at Christie’s or Sotheby’s, Gouzer’s app, Fair Warning, allows a select group of collectors to bid on one carefully-chosen work at a time. Sales on the app have set world auction records for contemporary artists including Elizabeth Peyton and Steven Shearer. In November, Fair Warning sold a 1974 Andy Warhol portrait of French film icon Brigitte Bardot for $16.7 million, the highest auction price recorded for the artist that year. Gouzer earned his reputation as the enfant terrible of the art market at Christie’s, where he was instrumental in coordinating the sale of Leonardo da Vinci’s Salvator Mundi in 2017, generating $450.3 million. Nearly a decade later, it remains the most expensive artwork ever sold at auction. Gouzer’s flair for showmanship continued in May with Fair Warning’s sale of Banksy’s Girl and Balloon on Found Landscape at Tiffany’s Fifth Avenue flagship in New York City, where it fetched $18 million.

entries.title: Marie Watt
entries.author: Taylor Dafoe
paragraphs: Marie Watt is one of the busiest artists you may not have heard of. Over the past five years, more than 20 museums have hosted shows focused on work by the 58-year-old, who is based in Portland, Ore. A citizen of the Seneca Nation, Watt creates sculptures, installations, and textiles using materials significant to her community, such as tin jingles: metal cones often sewn onto ceremonial dresses.

In June, she teamed up with artist Nick Cave to create a large-scale, site-specific sculpture at the Obama Presidential Center in Chicago. Collaboration is key to Watt, who is also known for organizing sewing circles. She sees these community events as both a means of creating art and a kind of art unto itself. “I'm interested in the relationship between part and whole in my work,” she says. “There is this conversation that happens when many hands come together to create a greater expression that couldn't have otherwise been realized.” Watt remains under the radar in some circles, in part because she works outside key art-market hubs and uses media that have long been undervalued by collectors. But she’s now frequently at the center of the national conversation—the ICA Boston will mount a mid-career retrospective of her work in fall 2027.

entries.title: Leo Villareal
entries.author: Olivia B. Waxman
paragraphs: Some of the brightest lights on the Manhattan skyline this year were designed by Leo Villareal, the architect behind an installation that sends waves of monochromatic flashes across the top of the new 60-story J.P. Morgan Chase headquarters, which opened last October. Villareal, 59, a Mexican American light artist, uses a custom software to program the building’s approximately 1.5 million LED lights nightly for a work he calls Celestial Passage. Around the globe, Villareal is making urban spaces twinkle. His display of 48,000 LEDs lights up the Bay Bridge, which connects Oakland to San Francisco in California, while his 3.2-mile-long Illuminated River in London bills itself as the world’s longest public art commission. The single lighting display connects the nine bridges on London’s Thames. At a time when it’s hard to get people to look up from their phones, Villareal’s projects are united by a desire to inspire awe and invite people to look more closely at the world around them.

entries.title: Danielle Mckinney
entries.author: Sarah Cascone
paragraphs: Danielle Mckinney took up painting after pandemic lockdown restrictions forced her to press pause on her street photography practice. The new works—quiet domestic scenes of Black women in the solitude of their own homes, relaxing in dimly lit, richly decorated rooms—drew on a long history of interior scenes in art. "Her work strikes such an emotional chord with people,” says the artist’s dealer, Marianne Boesky, who first discovered her on Instagram. Over the past six years, the gallery has placed Mckinney’s work in more than 30 museums (plus the collection of actor Josh Brolin). Getting a piece can be competitive: in March 2025, Mckinney’s painting of a woman lying across a patterned carpet more than quadrupled expectations, selling for $340,255 at auction. Her spring 2026 show at Marianne Boesky also sold out. The artist’s visions of pleasure and privacy will soon find an even larger audience. Her solo museum exhibition, “Shelter,” opened at the Norton Museum of Art in West Palm Beach, Fla., this spring and will travel to the New Orleans Museum of Art and the Studio Museum in Harlem.

entries.title: Tyler Mitchell
entries.author: Taylor Dafoe
paragraphs: Tyler Mitchell was just 23 when he photographed Beyoncé for Vogue in 2018, becoming the first Black artist to shoot the magazine’s cover. The image, now in the collection of the Smithsonian’s National Portrait Gallery, turned him into a voice of his generation overnight—and he’s only solidified that status since. The 31-year-old’s warm, tender portraits of Black people have endeared him to legendary artists like Carrie Mae Weems, Arthur Jafa, and Amy Sherald, all of whom he considers close friends. “My interest is in people,” he says. Like an increasing number of young photographers, Mitchell moves fluidly through the worlds of fashion, magazines, and art. He has shot campaigns for Ralph Lauren and Loewe, contributed photography to the catalogue of the Metropolitan Museum of Art’s exhibition “Superfine: Tailoring Black Style,” and mounted several solo museum shows. “My practice has evolved,” he says, “into something that is deeply flexible and porous and capacious in the way I think photography truly is.” On the horizon is a January show at Gagosian in Los Angeles and a pair of unannounced museum exhibitions, one on each side of the Atlantic.

entries.title: Atsuko Ninagawa
entries.author: Taylor Dafoe
paragraphs: With their surging participation costs and growing control over collectors’ calendars, art fairs can put galleries in a double bind. The ante is high, and so is the risk; a payout is by no means a guarantee when it can cost tens of thousands of dollars to enter a fair. This predicament drove gallerist Atsuko Ninagawa to co-found Art Week Tokyo, a decentralized event with the rare distinction of having no exhibitors’ fees. “In contrast to an art fair, where commercial pressures inevitably shape decision-making, doing away with participation fees helps to level the playing field for galleries,” says Ninagawa. “It sends a clear message that we want to shift the metric for evaluating an art event of this scope from making sales to making connections.” The five-day event, produced in collaboration with Art Basel and Japan Contemporary Art Platform, has proven instrumental in putting Japan’s once-insular contemporary art scene on the global map. Returning for its fifth edition in November, it will unfold across 53 Tokyo venues connected by a free bus service. Among the participants is Ninagawa’s own Take Ninagawa gallery, which will stage a show by the 91-year-old Japanese-Polish artist Koji Kamoji.

entries.title: Max Teicher
entries.author: Julie Davich
paragraphs: Max Teicher is an artist agent—a new kind of art-market professional. As brands, sports teams, and entertainers become increasingly interested in collaborating with visual artists, an agent like Teicher helps broker sponsorships, partnerships, and publishing deals on his clients’ behalf. “A lot of our job is bringing art outside the art world,” says Teicher. In exchange for a percentage of the project fee, most agents will broker any deal for an artist that does not involve selling art; that remains the purview of traditional galleries. Teicher launched 291 Agency in 2021, after 12 years at Gagosian. He credits artist Cecily Brown’s groundbreaking decision to work with his ex-Gagosian colleague—and now business partner—Andrea Crane with inspiring him to launch the agency, which is now one of the largest of a growing number in operation. Its staff of 20 supports about 40 clients, including sculptor Hank Willis Thomas and photographer Laurie Simmons. He’s signed on 10 artists and artists’ estates in the past year alone. At a time when some conventional galleries are struggling, agents are putting themselves forward as another way for artists to make it work.

entries.title: Mazdak Sanii
entries.author: Tim Schneider
paragraphs: Loads of industry professionals pay lip service to expanding access to art, but few back up the talk like Mazdak Sanii. As the chief executive and co-founder of the fast-growing prints and sculptural editions platform Avant Arte, he and his partners “want to help bring a new generation of people into discovering and collecting art for the first time,” he says. Avant Arte works with top artists like Jeff Koons, Ai Weiwei, and Cindy Sherman to create digital art and editions (a defined set of near-identical artworks). Then, they sell the work online for a fraction of what it would cost to buy an original by the same artist from a gallery. In less than a decade, more than 4 million people across over 100 countries have followed or subscribed to the platform, according to Sanii. After beginning as a publisher and distributor of prints, the firm vertically integrated by opening Make-Ready, one of the world's largest print studios, in London in 2023. They have also raised more than $20 million for arts institutions to date through collaborative projects, including with the Dia Art Foundation, the Guggenheim, LACMA, and MOMA PS1. In Sanii’s future, there is no patron as powerful as the public.
